But the State Government by an order to be published in the Official Gazette may extend the whole or any part of this Act to any presidency, State or place, and the whole or such portion of this Act as shall be specified in such order shall thereupon take effect in such presidency, State or place (Section 46).
key_provisions: Section 2: The entire police-establishment under a State Government shall be deemed to be one police force, formally enrolled, and constituted as ordered by the State Government. The pay and other conditions of service for members of the subordinate ranks shall be determined by the State Government.

Section 7: Inspector-General, Deputy Inspectors-General, Assistant Inspector-General, and District Superintendents of Police may dismiss, suspend, or reduce subordinate police officers for negligence or unfitness, or award punishments including fines (not exceeding one month's pay), confinement to quarters (not exceeding fifteen days), deprivation of good-conduct pay, or removal from office of distinction/emolument, subject to Article 311 of the Constitution and State Government rules.

Section 15A: Any inhabitant suffering injury (death, grievous hurt, property loss/damage) from misconduct of inhabitants in a proclaimed disturbed area may apply for compensation to the District Magistrate within one month. The District Magistrate, with State Government sanction and after inquiry, may declare injured persons, fix compensation, and assess payment proportions among inhabitants, provided the injury arose from a riot or unlawful assembly and the applicant was blameless.

Section 23: Every police-officer must promptly obey and execute lawful orders/warrants, collect/communicate intelligence affecting public peace, prevent offences/public nuisances, detect/apprehend offenders, and may, without warrant, enter and inspect drinking-shops, gaming-houses, or other resorts of disorderly characters.

Section 30: The District Superintendent or Assistant District Superintendent of Police may direct the conduct of public assemblies and processions, prescribe routes and times, and require a license for assemblies/processions likely to cause a breach of peace. A license may be issued defining conditions, with no fee charged.

Section 44: It shall be the duty of every officer in charge of a police-station to keep a general diary in such form as prescribed by the State Government, recording complaints, arrests, names, offences, property, and witnesses. The Magistrate of the district may inspect this diary.
administration: The superintendence of the police throughout a general police-district shall vest in and be exercised by the State Government. The administration of the police throughout the general police district shall be vested in an officer styled the Inspector-General of Police, and in such Deputy Inspectors-General and Assistant Inspectors-General as the State Government deems fit. The administration within the local jurisdiction of the Magistrate of the district shall be vested in a District Superintendent and Assistant District Superintendents, under the general control and direction of such Magistrate (Sections 3 and 4).

title: THE PARTITION ACT, 1893
purpose: To amend the law relating to partition.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India, and has been extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli (w.e.f. 1-7-1965), Pondicherry, and Sikkim (w.e.f. 1-9-1984). It applies to suits instituted before its commencement where no partition scheme has been finally approved by the court. It does not affect any local law providing for the partition of immoveable property paying revenue to Government.
key_provisions: Section 2: Power to court to order sale instead of division in partition suits, if a division cannot reasonably or conveniently be made and a sale would be more beneficial, on the request of shareholders interested individually or collectively to the extent of one moiety or upwards.

Section 3: Procedure when sharer undertakes to buy: If a shareholder applies for leave to buy at a valuation the share of a party asking for a sale, the court shall order a valuation of the share(s) in such manner as it may think fit and offer to sell at the ascertained price. If two or more shareholders apply, the court shall order a sale to the shareholder who offers to pay the highest price above the valuation.

Section 4: Partition suit by transferee of share in dwelling-house: Where a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family is transferred to a non-family member who sues for partition, the court shall, if a family member shareholder undertakes to buy, make a valuation of such share and direct its sale to that shareholder.

Section 6: Reserved bidding and bidding by shareholders: Every sale under section 2 shall be subject to a reserved bidding fixed by the court. Shareholders are at liberty to bid at the sale on terms regarding non-payment of deposit or setting off/accounting for purchase-money. If two or more persons, including a shareholder, advance the same sum, such bidding is deemed to be the shareholder's.

Section 7: Procedure to be followed in case of sales: For property sold under a decree or order of the High Court of Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay (original jurisdiction), the procedure of such court for the sale of property by the Registrar is adopted. For other courts, the procedure prescribed by the High Court by rules, or failing that, the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of sales in execution of decrees.

Section 8: Orders for sale to be deemed decrees: Any order for sale made by the court under section 2, 3 or 4 shall be deemed to be a decree within the meaning of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (14 of 1882).
administration: The Act is administered by 'the court' in partition suits. Sales procedures are governed by the High Courts of Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay (through their Registrar) for their original jurisdiction, or by rules prescribed by the High Court for other courts, or by the Code of Civil Procedure until such rules are made.

title: THE REVENUE COMMISSIONERS, BOMBAY ACT, 1842
purpose: An Act relative to the number and powers of the Revenue Commissioner under the Presidency of Bombay.
scope: The whole of the Territory composing the Presidency of Bombay.
key_provisions: Section I: So much of Regulation V, of 1830, of the Bombay Code, as provides that one Revenue Commissioner shall be appointed for the Territory subordinate to Bombay, and that the Southern Maharatta Country shall be excluded from his jurisdiction, is repealed.
Section II: One or more Revenue Commissioners shall be appointed for the whole of the Territory composing the Presidency of Bombay.
Section II: Each Revenue Commissioner shall be vested with all the powers possessed by the single Revenue Commissioner, under Regulation V, 1830.

Section II: Each Revenue Commissioner shall be empowered to act within the Presidency of Bombay, or over such portion as the Governor in Council of Bombay may, from time to time, prescribe by an Order published in the Gazette.
Section III: Each Revenue Commissioner shall have such number of Deputies and Assistants, as the Governor in Council may deem it expedient to appoint.
administration: The Governor in Council of Bombay

title: THE NORTHERN INDIA FERRIES ACT, 1878
purpose: To regulate ferries in Northern India, specifically in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, the Central Provinces, Assam, Delhi and Ajmer.
scope: It extends only to Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, the Central Provinces, Assam, Delhi and Ajmer.
key_provisions: Power to declare, establish, define and discontinue public ferries by the State Government via notification in the Official Gazette (Section 4).

Immediate superintendence of public ferries vested in the Magistrate of the district or an appointed officer (Section 6), or management vested in a municipality (Section 7) or District Council or District or Local Board (Section 7A).

Tolls of public ferries may be let by public auction for a term not exceeding five years with the approval of the Commissioner, or for any term with the previous sanction of the State Government (Section 8). Arrears due by the lessee are recoverable as if they were arrears of land-revenue (Section 9).

Power for the Commissioner of a division or an appointed officer to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette for public ferries (Section 12), including traffic regulation, toll letting, boat specifications, crew, and operating hours. Rules for private ferries can also be made for the maintenance of order and safety of passengers and property (Section 19).

Prohibition against establishing, maintaining, or working a private ferry to or from any point within a distance of two miles from the limits of a public ferry without the sanction of the Magistrate of the district or an appointed officer (Section 13).

Penalties for various offenses including neglecting to affix/maintain table of tolls (Section 21), taking unauthorized tolls or causing delay (Section 22), breaching rules (Section 23), maintaining a private ferry within prohibited limits (Section 26), and rash navigation (Section 28).
administration: The State Government is responsible for declaring, establishing, defining, and discontinuing public ferries (Section 4), appointing officers for superintendence (Section 6), directing management by municipalities (Section 7) or District Councils/Boards (Section 7A), sanctioning toll letting (Section 8), cancelling leases (Section 10), fixing toll rates (Section 15), and delegating powers (Section 35). The Commissioner of the Division, or an appointed officer, makes rules for public ferries (Section 12) and private ferries (Section 19), and approves toll letting (Section 8). The Magistrate of the District has immediate superintendence of public ferries (Section 6), recovers arrears (Section 9), handles compensation claims (Section 5), and enforces penalties (Sections 24, 31). Police may arrest without warrant for specific offenses (Section 29), and Magistrates can try offenses summarily (Section 30).

title: THE BENGAL EMBANKMENT ACT, 1855
purpose: Provision should be made for the better supervision and protection of embankments in the Territories under the Government of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, as existing regulations have been found ineffectual for these purposes (Preamble).
scope: The Act applies to "public embankments" in the Territories under the Government of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal. A "public embankment" is defined as an embankment for the purpose of excluding or retaining water, which is now kept up, or may hereafter be kept up, by the officers of the Government, at the expense either of Government or of any private person (Section II).
key_provisions: Section I: Repeals Regulation VI. of 1806 and Regulation XI. of 1829, so far as they relate to the said Territories, except as to acts done, offenses committed, and liabilities incurred before the passing of this Act.

Section V: Establishes a procedure for the Superintendent of Embankments to cause works (taking charge of embankments, removing private embankments, changing lines, or making new ones) to be executed. The Superintendent must give written notice to the Collector, who issues a proclamation (published not less than fifteen days before the hearing) for interested parties to appear and object. The Collector hears objections and communicates them to the Superintendent. If they agree, an order is passed; if they differ, the case is referred to the Commissioner of Revenue for a final order. Orders by the Superintendent are appealable to the Commissioner of Revenue, and Commissioner's orders are appealable to the Board of Revenue, provided the appeal is presented within one month from the order date. Such orders are final and not open to revision by any Civil Court, subject to appeal and Government control.

Section VII: Provides for compensation for damages sustained when the Superintendent enlarges or changes the line of an embankment, makes a new one, or causes removal. Claims must be preferred to the Collector within twelve months after the work. If the claim is admitted by Revenue authorities and the amount is not agreed upon, it is settled by arbitration. Unless the Collector and claimant concur on a single arbitrator, each appoints one in writing. If multiple claimants cannot agree, the Collector chooses one by lot from their nominations. If more than one arbitrator is appointed, they nominate a third within seven days, or the Collector appoints one. The Collector can enforce arbitrator attendance and provide information. Awards specify compensation and entitled parties, and proceedings are deposited in the Collector's office. Awards can only be reversed or altered by a Civil Court on grounds of corruption or misconduct, with suits to set aside an award instituted within three months from the award date.

Section VIII: Outlines the process for land-holders to apply for sluices in public embankments for drainage or irrigation. Applications are made in writing to the Collector, detailing the land and willingness to defray costs (up to half for state-maintained, or whole/part for others). The Collector transmits the application to the Officer in charge of embankments, who reports to the Superintendent of Embankments with a plan and estimate if unobjectionable. The Superintendent's order is final. If approved, the applicant enters a written agreement to defray costs, and the Collector issues a certificate for construction.

Section XII: Details the procedure for the removal of houses, huts, or other buildings situated between a public embankment and the river, deemed necessary by the Superintendent. The Superintendent reports to the Collector, who issues a notice and proclamation (not less than fifteen days from proclamation date) for claimants to appear before a jury. The jury, consisting of a Deputy Collector or Principal Officer and three respectable inhabitants, determines the value of the buildings and, if disputed, the rights of claimants. The jury assesses value separately, with the Deputy Collector/officer having a casting vote in case of a tie. The award, containing a schedule of buildings, assessed value, and entitled persons, is final and conclusive, though persons not present or whose claim was set aside may sue for property value against the recipient of payment.

Sections XV, XVI, XVII: Establishes penalties for various offenses. Section XV imposes imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to two hundred rupees (or both) for wilfully obstructing authorized persons in removing or levelling any embankment, house, hut, or other building. Section XVI imposes imprisonment up to one year or a fine up to two hundred rupees (or both) for wilfully cutting through, destroying, or opening sluices/water-courses in any embankment; for insufficient punishment, the offender may be committed to the Sessions Court, facing imprisonment up to seven years or a fine (or both). Section XVII imposes simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to two hundred rupees (or both) for other wilful damages to public embankments, such as making unauthorized dams, altering banks, removing earth, grazing cattle, or driving stakes.
administration: The Act is administered by the Superintendent of Embankments, who is entrusted with the superintendence of public embankments (Section III). The Collector of the district plays a significant role in issuing notices, hearing objections, managing compensation claims, facilitating arbitration, processing sluice applications, and overseeing the removal of buildings (Sections V, VII, VIII, XI, XII, XIII, XIV). Appeals against orders are handled by the Commissioner of Revenue and the Board of Revenue (Section V, XI). Deputy and Assistant Magistrates have jurisdiction over offenses under the Act (Section XVIII), and Darogahs and other Police Officers are empowered to inquire into specified offenses (Section XIX).

title: THE MARRIED WOMEN’S PROPERTY ACT, 1874
purpose: To explain and amend the law relating to certain married women, to make provision for the enjoyment of wages and earnings by women married before January 1, 1866, and for insurances on lives by persons married before or after that day, and to address related liabilities and claims by or against such wives.
scope: Extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Does not apply to any married woman who, or whose husband, at the time of marriage, professed the Hindu, Muhammadan, Buddhist, Sikh or Jaina religion. The State Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, exempt or revoke exemptions for members of any race, sect or tribe from the Act's provisions.
key_provisions: Section 4: The wages and earnings of any married woman acquired or gained by her after the passing of this Act, in any employment, occupation or trade carried on by her and not by her husband, and also any money or other property so acquired by her through the exercise of any literary, artistic or scientific skill, and all savings from and investments of such wages, earnings and property, shall be deemed to be her separate property, and her receipts alone shall be good discharges for such wages, earnings and property.

Section 5: Any married woman may effect a policy of insurance on her own behalf and independently of her husband; and the same and all benefit thereof, if expressed on the face of it to be so effected, shall ensure as her separate property, and the contract evidenced by such policy shall be as valid as if made with an unmarried woman.

Section 6(1): A policy of insurance effected by any married man on his own life, and expressed on the face of it to be for the benefit of his wife, or of his wife and children, or any of them, shall ensure and be deemed to be a trust for their benefit. When the sum secured by the policy becomes payable, it shall, unless special trustees are duly appointed, be paid to the Official Trustee of the State in which the office at which the insurance was effected is situated, to be held upon the trusts expressed in the policy.

Section 7: A married woman may maintain a suit in her own name for the recovery of property which is her separate property, and shall have the same remedies, both civil and criminal, against all persons for its protection and security, as if she were unmarried, and shall be liable to such suits, processes and orders in respect of such property as if she were unmarried.

Section 9: A husband married after December 31, 1865, shall not by reason only of such marriage be liable to the debts of his wife contracted before marriage, but the wife shall be liable to be sued for, and shall, to the extent of her separate property, be liable to satisfy such debts as if she had continued unmarried.

Section 10: Where a woman is a trustee, executrix or administratrix, either before or after marriage, her husband shall not, unless he acts or intermeddles in the trust or administration, be liable for any breach of trust committed by her, or for any misapplication, loss or damage to the estate of the deceased caused or made by her, or for any loss to such estate arising from her neglect to get in any part of the property of deceased.
administration: The State Government may from time to time, by order, either retrospectively or prospectively, exempt from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this Act the members of any race, sect or tribe, or revoke any such order, with all orders and revocations published in the Official Gazette. The Official Trustee of the State is designated to receive and hold sums from insurance policies effected by husbands for the benefit of their wives or children, unless special trustees are duly appointed.

title: THE PRISONS ACT, 1894
purpose: To amend the law relating to Prisons and to provide rules for the regulation of such prison.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. It does not apply to civil jails in the State of Bombay as it existed immediately before the 1st November, 1956 outside the city of Bombay, which continue to be administered under sections 9 and 16 of Bombay Act 2 of 1874.
key_provisions: Section 4: The State Government shall provide accommodation for prisoners in prisons constructed and regulated to comply with the Act's requisitions for prisoner separation.

Section 24: Upon admission, prisoners shall be searched for weapons and prohibited articles. Every criminal prisoner shall be examined by the Medical Officer, who records their health, marks, fitness for labour, and observations in a book kept by the Jailer. Female prisoners' search and examination are carried out by the matron under the Medical Officer's orders.

Section 27: Prisoners must be separated as follows: females from males (in separate buildings or parts), male prisoners under twenty-one from other prisoners (and those of puberty age from those not), unconvicted criminal prisoners from convicted criminal prisoners, and civil prisoners from criminal prisoners.

Section 45: Defines specific acts as prison-offences when committed by a prisoner, including wilful disobedience to prison regulations, assault, use of insulting language, wilfully disabling oneself from labour, contumaciously refusing to work, tampering with prison property, receiving prohibited articles, feigning illness, and conspiring to escape.

Section 46: The Superintendent may punish prison-offences by: (1) a formal warning; (2) change of labour to a more irksome or severe form; (3) hard labour for up to seven days for convicted criminal prisoners not sentenced to rigorous imprisonment; (4) loss of privileges under the remission system; (5) substitution of coarse fabric for clothing; (6) imposition of handcuffs; (7) imposition of fetters; (8) separate confinement for up to three months; (9) penal diet; (10) cellular confinement for up to fourteen days; (11) penal diet combined with cellular confinement; (12) whipping (not exceeding thirty stripes), with provisos against applying handcuffs, fetters, or whipping to female or civil prisoners.

Section 59: The State Government may make rules consistent with this Act by notification in the Official Gazette for purposes including: defining prison-offences and their classification, fixing punishments, regulating the use of arms against prisoners, classifying prisons and detention places, governing prisons and appointing officers, regulating food, bedding, clothing, and employment of prisoners, defining prohibited articles, classifying and regulating labour, regulating confinement in fetters, classifying and separating prisoners, preparing history-tickets, selecting prisoner officers, regulating prisoner transfers, treating criminal lunatics, regulating transmission of appeals and petitions, appointing prison visitors, and extending provisions to subsidiary jails.
administration: The State Government provides accommodation for prisoners (Section 4) and makes rules for the administration of prisons (Section 59). An Inspector General is appointed for the territories subject to each State Government to exercise general control and superintendence of all prisons (Section 5). Superintendents manage individual prisons in all matters relating to discipline, labour, expenditure, punishment, and control, subject to the orders of the Inspector General (Section 11).

title: THE WASTE LANDS (CLAIMS) ACT, 1863
purpose: To make special provision for the speedy adjudication of claims which may be preferred to waste lands proposed to be sold, or otherwise dealt with, on account of the State Government, and of objections taken to the sale or other disposition of such lands.
scope: The Act applies to claims preferred to waste lands proposed to be sold, or otherwise dealt with, on account of the State Government, and objections taken to the sale or other disposition of such lands. It also covers claims to land, or compensation or damages in respect of land, sold or otherwise dealt with as waste land. The Act has been declared to be in force in all part A States except the Scheduled Districts, and extended to new Provinces and Merged States, and to the States of Manipur, Tripura and Vindhya Pradesh.
key_provisions: Section 1: The Collector of the District shall make an inquiry into any claim or objection to waste land proposed to be sold or dealt with, if preferred within the advertised period, which shall not be less than three months.

Section 5: If the Collector rejects a claim or objection, or orders land sold subject to conditions, a copy of the order is delivered to the claimant/objector. If they do not give notice of intent to contest within one week (or extended time), the order is final. If notice is given, the Collector reports to the Board of Revenue (or superior Revenue Authority), which may confirm, modify, or reverse the order.

Section 7: For the investigation and trial of claims, the Local Government shall constitute a Special Court in every District, consisting of an uneven number of persons (not less than three), including the Judge of the District or the Officer presiding in the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction.
Section 14: No appeal shall lie from any decision or order passed under this Act, nor shall any such decision or order be open to revision.

Section 18: No claim to any land, or to compensation or damages in respect of any land, sold or otherwise dealt with as waste land on account of the State Government, shall be received after the expiration of three years from the date on which such land shall have been delivered by the Government to the purchaser, or otherwise dealt with.

Section 19: If a claim to land that has been sold is established by the Court, the claimant shall not be awarded possession of the land but shall receive from the State Government Treasury, by way of compensation, a sum equal to the price at which the land was sold, in addition to the costs of suit.
administration:
The administration of this Act involves:
*   **Collector of the District (or other Officer performing duties of a Collector of Land Revenue)**: Conducts initial inquiries into claims or objections (Section 1, 2). Postpones sale during inquiry (Section 3). Stops sale if claim is established (Section 4). Delivers orders and reports to the superior Revenue Authority (Section 5). Appears as defendant in suits under Section V (Section 10).
*   **Board of Revenue (or other superior Revenue Authority)**: Receives reports from the Collector and may confirm, modify, or reverse the Collector's order (Section 5).
*   **Local Government**: May order a suit to be brought to try a claim admitted by the Collector (Section 6). Constitutes Special Courts (Section 7). Appoints officers to appear as plaintiff in suits under Section VI (Section 10).
*   **Special Courts**: Constituted by the Local Government in every District for the investigation and trial of claims, consisting of an uneven number of persons, not less than three, including the District Judge or presiding officer of the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction (Section 7). These Courts hear suits, examine parties and witnesses, and pass orders (Section 12, 13).
*   **High Court of Judicature (or highest Civil Court of Appeal and Revision)**: Receives references from Special Courts on questions of law, usage, or construction of documents, especially those involving principles of general importance or rights of a class (Section 15).
*   **State Government**: Its powers and duties under sections 6, 10, 22, and 23 may be exercised by the Board of Revenue or the Financial Commissioner in a State where such bodies exist (Section 23A).

title: THE PENSIONS’ ACT, 1871
purpose: to consolidate and amend the law relating to pensions and grants by Government of money or land -revenue
scope: In so far as it relates to Union pensions, it extends to the whole of India and in so far as it relates to other pensions, it extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States.
key_provisions: Section 4: Bar of suits relating to pensions. Except as hereinafter provided, no Civil Court shall entertain any suit relating to any pension or grant of money or land-revenue conferred or made by the Government or by any former Government.

Section 5: Claims to be made to Collector, Deputy Commissioner or other authorized officer. Any person having a claim relating to any such pension or grant may prefer such claim to the Collector of the District or Deputy Commissioner or other officer authorized in this behalf by the appropriate Government, who shall dispose of such claim in accordance with rules prescribed by the Chief Revenue Authority, subject to the general control of the appropriate Government.

Section 6: Civil Court empowered to take cognizance of such claims. A Civil Court may take cognizance of a claim upon receiving a certificate from the Collector, Deputy Commissioner or other authorized officer that the case may be tried, but shall not make any order or decree affecting the Government's liability to pay the pension or grant.

Section 10: Commutation of pensions. The appropriate Government may, with the consent of the holder, order the whole or any part of his pension or grant of money or land-revenue to be commuted for a lump sum on such terms as may seem fit.

Section 11: Exemption of pension from attachment. No pension granted or continued by Government on political considerations, or on account of past services or present infirmities or as a compassionate allowance, and no money due or to become due on account of any such pension or allowance, shall be liable to seizure, attachment or sequestration by process of any Court at the instance of a creditor.

Section 12A: Nomination by pensioner to receive moneys outstanding on account of pension. A pensioner may nominate another person, in such manner and form as prescribed by Central Government rules, to receive all unpaid moneys on account of such pension after the pensioner's death. The nominee is entitled to receive these moneys to the exclusion of all other persons, unless the nominee predeceases the pensioner and a provision for another person has been made in the nomination.
administration: Claims and payments relating to pensions and grants are handled by the Collector of the District, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officers. The Chief Controlling Revenue Authority in each State, with the consent of the appropriate Government, is empowered to make rules concerning payment procedures, identity inquiries, record keeping, and certificates. The Central Government is authorized to make rules regarding the manner and form for nominations under Section 12A, including cancellation, variation, and provisions for alternative recipients. All such rules are to be published in the local official Gazette, and rules made by the Central Government or by a Chief Controlling Revenue Authority with Central Government consent must be laid before each House of Parliament.

title: The Oudh Estates’ Act, 1869
purpose: To define the rights of Taluqdárs and others in certain estates in Oudh, and to regulate the succession thereto, and to prevent doubts as to the nature of such rights and the course of succession, and to provide for other connected matters.
scope: This Act extends only to the estates hereinafter referred to, which means the taluqa or immoveable property acquired or held by a Taluqdár or Grantee in the manner mentioned in section three, section four, or section five, or the immoveable property conferred by a special grant of the British Government upon a Grantee.
key_provisions: Every Taluqdár with whom a summary settlement was made between April 1, 1858, and October 10, 1859, or who received a Taluqdárí sanad after April 1, 1858, acquires a permanent, heritable, and transferable right in their estate, subject to conditions in the Governor General's orders of October 10 and 19, 1859, and the sanad (Section 3).

Within six months of the Act's passing, the Chief Commissioner of Oudh shall prepare six lists of Taluqdárs and Grantees, including those with primogeniture succession or subject to Section 23. These lists, once approved by the Chief Commissioner, shall be published in the Gazette of India and are generally not alterable, except as per Sections 30 or 31, or by order of the Governor General in Council for omissions/errors (Sections 8 & 9).

Taluqdárs, Grantees, and their heirs/legatees of sound mind and not minors, may transfer their estate or interest therein during their lifetime by sale, exchange, mortgage, lease, or gift, and may bequeath by will, provided the transfer or will is not caused by fraud, coercion, or undue importunity (Section 11).

A Taluqdár, Grantee, heir, or legatee may not give or bequeath their estate to any person not an intestate successor under this Act or ordinary law, or a younger son (if listed in list 3 or 5), unless by an instrument of gift or will executed and attested not less than three months before death, and registered within one month of execution (Section 13).

For intestate Taluqdárs or Grantees named in lists 2, 3, or 5, or their heirs/legatees, the estate descends primarily to the eldest son and his male lineal descendants, then to other sons, then to a daughter's son treated as his own, then to an adopted son (by registered writing), then to brothers, then to the first-married widow for life, and so forth, as detailed in the section (Section 22).

Upon the death of a Taluqdár, Grantee, heir, or legatee, the person in possession of the estate is liable to pay annuities to surviving relatives (grandparents, parents, widows, brothers, minor sons, nephews, unmarried daughters, widows of sons/brothers, inferior widows) who lived with the deceased and lack other adequate maintenance, with amounts and durations specified in Sections 25-28 (Section 24).
administration: The Chief Commissioner of Oudh is responsible for preparing and approving lists of Taluqdárs and Grantees, and for receiving declarations to alter succession rules. The Governor General of India in Council provides instructions for list preparation and can order corrections to lists. The Financial Commissioner of Oudh is responsible for approving and filing awards as to compensation and maintenance.

title: THE GENERAL CLAUSES ACT, 1897
purpose: To consolidate and extend the General Clauses Acts, 1868 (1 of 1868) and 1887 (1 of 1887).
scope: This Act applies to itself, and to all Central Acts and Regulations made after its commencement, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context. Certain definitions also apply to previous enactments and Indian Laws. It provides general rules of construction, definitions, and provisions regarding powers, functionaries, and orders, rules, etc., made under enactments.
key_provisions: Section 3. Definitions: Provides definitions for numerous terms (e.g., "abet", "act", "affidavit", "Central Act", "Central Government", "document", "enactment", "good faith", "immovable property", "offence", "person", "rule", "State", "Union territory", "year") to be used in this Act and in all Central Acts and Regulations made after its commencement, unless repugnant to the subject or context.

Section 6. Effect of repeal: Specifies that unless a different intention appears, the repeal of any enactment by this Act or any Central Act or Regulation made after its commencement shall not revive anything not in force, affect previous operation, affect any acquired right/privilege/obligation/liability, affect any incurred penalty/forfeiture/punishment, or affect any investigation/legal proceeding/remedy related to these, allowing such actions to be instituted, continued, or enforced as if the repealing Act or Regulation had not been passed.

Section 10. Computation of time: States that if an act or proceeding directed or allowed to be done in any Court or office on a certain day or within a prescribed period falls on a day when the Court or office is closed, it shall be considered done in due time if done on the next day the Court or office is open. This does not apply to acts or proceedings governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1877 (15 of 1877).

Section 16. Power to appoint to include power to suspend or dismiss: Confers that where a power to make any appointment is granted by any Central Act or Regulation, the authority having the power to make the appointment shall also have the power to suspend or dismiss any person appointed, unless a different intention appears.

Section 23. Provisions applicable to making of rules or bye-laws after previous publication: Outlines the procedure for making rules or bye-laws subject to previous publication. This includes publishing a draft for affected persons, specifying a date for consideration, considering objections/suggestions received before that date, and deeming publication in the Official Gazette as conclusive proof that the rule or bye-law has been duly made.

Section 26. Provision as to offences punishable under two or more enactments: Stipulates that where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, the offender may be prosecuted and punished under any of those enactments, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence.
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE INDIAN TREASURE -TROVE ACT, 1878
purpose: To amend the law relating to treasure-trove.
scope: It extends to the whole of India except "the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States". The Act has been extended to various other territories and amended by several State Acts.
key_provisions: Section 4: Whenever any treasure exceeding in amount or value ten rupees is found, the finder shall, as soon as practicable, give to the Collector notice in writing of its nature, amount/value, place, and date of finding, and either deposit the treasure in the nearest Government treasury or give security to produce it.

Section 5: On receiving notice under section 4, the Collector shall publish a notification requiring all claimants to appear personally or by agent before the Collector on a day and at a place mentioned, such day not being earlier than four months or later than six months after the publication date.

Section 9: The Collector may declare treasure to be ownerless if there's no reason to believe it was hidden within one hundred years, or if a suit to establish right is not instituted within the fixed period, or if such suit's claim is finally rejected. Any person aggrieved by such a declaration may appeal within two months to the Chief Controlling Revenue authority.

Section 12: If only one person other than the finder claims as owner of the place and their claim is undisputed, the Collector shall divide the treasure, allotting three-fourths to the finder and the residue to the claimant, unless an agreement exists. The Collector may also allot the whole or more than a share by payment or sell by public auction and divide proceeds.

Section 16: The Collector may, after a declaration under section 9 and before delivery or division, acquire the treasure or a portion on behalf of the Government by paying the entitled persons a sum equal to the value of the materials plus one-fifth of such value.

Section 20: If the finder fails to give notice, deposit, or security as required by section 4, or alters the treasure to conceal its identity, their entitled share shall vest in Government, and they shall be punished with imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, on conviction before a Magistrate.
administration: The Act is primarily administered by the Collector, who conducts inquiries, issues notifications, determines claims, and divides or acquires treasure. Appeals against the Collector's declaration are made to the Chief Controlling Revenue authority. The State Government has the power to make rules consistent with the Act. Penalties are enforced on conviction before a Magistrate.

title: THE CHUTIA NAGPUR ENCUMBERED ESTATES ACT, 1876
purpose: To provide for the relief of holders of land in Chutia Nagpur who may be in debt, and whose immoveable property may be subject to mortgages, charges and liens.
scope: The Act applies to holders of land in Chutia Nagpur who are in debt, specifically concerning their immoveable property subject to mortgages, charges, and liens, excluding debts due or liabilities incurred to Government.
key_provisions: Vesting of Management and its Legal Effects (Sections 2, 3): Upon written application, the Commissioner, with the Lieutenant-Governor's previous consent, may appoint a Manager and vest in him the management of the holder's immoveable property. This order, published in the Calcutta Gazette, bars all pending civil suits regarding the debts, nullifies processes/executions/attachments, frees the holder and heir from arrest for prior debts, exempts their movable property from attachment/sale for prior debts, renders them incompetent to mortgage/charge/lease/alienate immoveable property, exempts immoveable property from attachment/sale (except for government debts), and incapacitates them from entering pecuniary contracts.

Manager's Duties and Debt Settlement Procedure (Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11): The Manager receives rents/profits and pays government revenue, superior landlord's rent, maintenance, repairs, management costs, and then debts. The Manager must publish a notice in English, Urdu, and Hindi, calling for claims within three months from the date of publication. Claimants must provide full particulars and documents; failure to produce documents may lead to their exclusion as evidence. Debts not duly notified within three months (or an extended nine months with proof of inability to comply) are barred. The Manager determines the amount of principal debts, liabilities, and interest according to rules, and prepares a scheme for settlement of debts for Commissioner's approval.

Manager's Powers (Sections 16, 17, 18): The Manager has the same powers as the property holder for realizing rents/profits. The Manager may apply to the Court of the Deputy Commissioner to remove a mortgagee or conditional vendee in possession. The Manager has the power to demise (lease) property for any term not exceeding twenty years. With the Commissioner's previous assent, the Manager can raise money for debt settlement by mortgaging property for a term not exceeding twenty years or by selling a portion (with the previous consent of the holder and heir) by public auction or private contract.

Appeals Process (Section 10): An appeal against any refusal, admission, determination, or order under sections six, seven, eight or nine shall lie, if preferred within six weeks from the date thereof, to the Deputy Commissioner within whose jurisdiction the property is situate. If the Deputy Commissioner is the Manager, the appeal lies to the Commissioner. A further appeal shall lie from any decision of the Deputy Commissioner, if preferred within six weeks of the date of his decision, to the Commissioner.

Restoration of Owner and Revival of Barred Proceedings (Section 12): When all debts are discharged, or if the Commissioner thinks that the provisions of this Act should not continue to apply within six months after the publication of the vesting order, the holder or heir is restored to possession. If restored under the latter circumstance, the previously barred proceedings, processes, executions, attachments (from Section 3), and debts (barred by Section 7) are revived, and dispossessed mortgagees/conditional vendees (under Section 16) are reinstated, unless their claim is satisfied. The time intervening between such restoration and the publication of the vesting order shall be excluded for calculating periods of limitation.

Rule-Making Authority (Section 19): The Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal may, from time to time, make rules consistent with this Act to regulate security from subordinate officers, notices and their publication, procedures for determining debts and liabilities (under Section 8), allowance of interest, order of paying debts, and general guidance for officers. Such rules, when approved by the Governor General in Council and published in the Calcutta Gazette, shall have the force of law.
administration: The Act is administered by a Manager, appointed by the Commissioner with the previous consent of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal. The Commissioner oversees the Manager's actions, approves schemes, and hears appeals. The Deputy Commissioner receives applications, sanctions inquiries, and hears appeals. The Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal has the power to make rules, which require approval from the Governor General in Council.

title: ACT NO.13 OF 1842: An Act to enable the holders of Revenue which has been alienated to them by the State, to collect that Revenue within the Presidency of Bombay.
purpose: To authorize the grant by the Governor in Council of Bombay, at his discretion, of Commissions to certain Jageerdars, and others, by virtue of which such persons shall possess increased powers for collecting the Revenue due to them.
scope: This Act applies to Jageerdars, Surinjamdars, Inamdars, or other persons holding Lands or Villages the Revenue of which has been alienated to them by the State, within the Presidency of Bombay. The power conferred by such Commission extends to the enforcement of the payment of the Revenue of the current season and of the season next immediately preceding, and not to that of former years.
key_provisions: It shall be lawful for the Governor in Council of Bombay to grant any Jageerdar, Surinjamdar, Inamdar, or other person holding Lands or Villages the Revenue of which has been alienated to him by the State, a Commission conferring upon him authority for the collection of such Revenue by the powers hereinafter mentioned, or such of them as shall be specified in the Commission in addition to the powers now exercisable by law. (Section I)

Such Commission, which shall be drawn out according to the form of the annexed Schedule A, shall be granted or withheld, and, when granted, shall be liable to be withdrawn at the pleasure of Government, and may be issued to one or more Agents of such holder of alienated Revenue as well as to the holder in person. (Section II)

The holder of such Commission shall have authority to demand security for the payment of the Revenue, in respect of the Lands or Villages specified in the Commission, and if the same be not furnished, to take such precaution as the Collector is authorized to make under Section XI, Regulation XVII, of 1827, Bombay Code. (Section III)

The holder of any such Commission shall be authorized to attach the property of persons making default in the payment of such Revenue, making an immediate report to the Collector or his Assistant. Should the demand appear just, the Collector or his Assistant shall give orders for the sale of such property, conducted agreeably to the Provisions of clause VII, Section XII, Regulation XVII, of 1827, Bombay Code, except when the holder is a Jageerdar, Surinjamdar or Inamdar vested by Regulation XIII, of 1830, with Civil jurisdiction, in which case the sale shall be conducted by him or his Agents. (Section V)

All compulsory process under this Act shall cease on the alleged defaulter furnishing security to the holder of the Commission or to the Collector or Assistant Collector of the District, to institute a suit within 15 days in a competent Court for the purpose of trying the demand and to pay the amount which may be decreed against him with costs and interest. Suits in which any of the privileged classes established by Regulation XXIX, of 1827, Sections III, and IV, and by Regulation VII, of 1830, Bombay Code, may be the defendant, shall be tried before the Collector and his Assistants. (Section VI)

The enforcement of a demand by any holder of a Commission under this Act of an excess of rent or Revenue beyond the amount due as provided shall be deemed extortion, and the person against whom such demand shall have been enforced shall obtain upon any judgement being passed after regular or summary trial three times the amount of any such excessive demand as damages for the same. (Section VII)
administration: The Governor in Council of Bombay is responsible for granting and withdrawing Commissions. The Collector or his Assistant are involved in receiving reports of property attachments, ordering sales, and trying certain suits involving privileged classes. The holder of the Commission, or their Agents, are empowered to collect revenue and enforce provisions under the Act.

title: THE MADRAS CITY CIVIL COURT ACT, 1892
purpose: To establish an additional Civil Court for the City of Madras.
scope: The Act establishes the Madras City Civil Court with jurisdiction to receive, try, and dispose of all suits and other proceedings of a civil nature not exceeding two thousand five hundred rupees in value and arising within the City of Madras. This excludes suits cognizable by the High Court (as a Court of Admiralty, Vice-Admiralty, Colonial Court of Admiralty, or having testamentary, intestate, or matrimonial jurisdiction), the Court for the relief of insolvent debtors, or the Small Cause Court. The 'City of Madras' means the area within the local limits of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the High Court. Valuation of immoveable property for jurisdictional purposes is fixed according to the Court-fees Act, 1870 (7 of 1870), section 7, clause v.
key_provisions: Section 3: The Local Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, establish the Madras City Civil Court with jurisdiction for civil suits and proceedings not exceeding two thousand five hundred rupees in value arising within the City of Madras, excluding specific High Court, insolvent debtors' court, or Small Cause Court matters.
Section 4: The Local Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, appoint Judges to the City Court and may, for misconduct, suspend or remove any Judge by a like notification.

Section 5: Every person appointed a Judge of the City Court shall, by virtue of office, be a Judge of the Small Cause Court for cognizable cases, and shall perform duties required by the Chief Justice of the High Court.

Section 13: Whenever any suit or proceeding in the City Court is settled by agreement of the parties before issues have been settled or any evidence recorded, half the amount of the institution fees paid by the plaintiff shall be repaid to him by the Court.

Section 15: The High Court is authorized to hear appeals from the City Court, and the period of limitation for such appeals shall be the same as for appeals from a High Court decree or order in its original jurisdiction.

Section 16 (Proviso 2): Any Judge of the High Court may, at any stage of a suit or proceeding pending in the High Court, order its transfer to the City Court if it is within the City Court's jurisdiction and should be tried therein.
administration: The Local Government establishes the City Court, appoints, suspends, and removes its Judges, and sanctions the appointment of ministerial officers. When the City Court has more than one Judge, the Local Government appoints a principal Judge who arranges the distribution of court business. The principal Judge also directs ministerial duties and, subject to the control of the High Court, may suspend, remove, or fine ministerial officers. The High Court administers the law for questions arising in suits, prescribes process-fees with the approval of the Governor of Fort St. George in Council, and its Chief Justice may require City Court Judges to perform duties of a Small Cause Court Judge. The Local Government also prescribes the form and dimensions of the court's seal and approves its annual list of holidays and vacations.

title: THE INDIAN TOLLS ACT, 1864
purpose: To amend Act 8 of 1851 (for enabling Government to levy Tolls on Public Roads and Bridges).
scope: The Act is in force in or has been extended to the Santhal Parganas, the C. P. and the Sambalpur District, the Districts of Hazaribagh, Lohardaga (now the Ranchi District), Manbhum, Pargana Dhalbhum and the Kolhan in the District of Singbhum, the District of Lahaul, Coorg, Ajmer-Merwara, the Scheduled Districts in Vizagapatam and Ganjam, the District of Darjeeling, the Union territory of Pondicherry, and the Punjab. The State Government may extend this Act to any place in which Act 8 of 1851 is in force; and the State Government of any place in which Act 8 of 1851 is not in force may extend the said Act 8 of 1851 and this Act to such place.
key_provisions: Collectors of tolls may compound for tolls leviable under Act 8 of 1851 or this Act for any period not exceeding one year with any person for a certain sum to be paid by such person for himself or for any vehicle or animal kept by him, in lieu of the rates of toll authorised to be levied under the said Act 8 of 1851 (Section 2).
The State Government may extend this Act to any place in which Act 8 of 1851 is in force (Section 3).
The State Government of any place in which Act 8 of 1851 is not in force may extend the said Act 8 of 1851 and this Act to such place (Section 3).
The Act serves to amend Act 8 of 1851, which provides authority for the Government to levy Tolls on Public Roads and Bridges (Preamble).
administration: The State Government is empowered to extend the Act. The collection of tolls and the compounding process are managed by 'any person entrusted with the management of the collection of tolls under Act 8 of 1851'.

title: THE RELIGIOUS ENDOWMENTS ACT, 1863
purpose: To enable the Government to divest itself of the management of Religious Endowments, by relieving the Boards of Revenue and local Agents from duties related to the superintendence of lands granted for the support of Mosques or Hindu Temples and for other religious uses, the appropriation of endowments, the repair and preservation of connected buildings, and the appointment of trustees or managers thereof.
scope: The Act applies to mosques, temples, and other religious establishments to which the provisions of Regulation XIX, 1810 (Bengal Code) and Regulation VII, 1817 (Madras Code) were applicable. It has been extended to various Scheduled Districts and regions including Kanara, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, and Section 22 applies to the whole of India except Part B States. The Act does not apply to Hindu religious endowments in Madras (after 1927) and Orissa (after 1939), religious trusts in Bihar (after 1951), or any wakf to which the Wakf Act, 1954 (Act 29 of 1954) applies.
key_provisions: Section 3: The State Government shall, as soon as possible after the passing of this Act, make special provision for every mosque, temple or other religious establishment where the nomination of the trustee, manager or superintendent is vested in, or exercised by, or subject to confirmation of, the Government or any public officer.

Section 4: The State Government shall, as soon as possible after the passing of this Act, transfer to the existing trustee, manager or superintendent all landed or other property under the superintendence or in possession of the Board of Revenue or any local agent, belonging to such religious establishment, whose nomination is not vested in or confirmed by the Government or any public officer. Upon transfer, the powers and responsibilities of the Board of Revenue and local agents cease.

Section 5: In case of a vacancy in the office of a trustee, manager, or superintendent to whom property was transferred under Section 4, and a dispute arises regarding succession, any interested person may apply to the Civil Court to appoint a manager to act until a successor establishes their right by suit. The appointed manager shall exercise all powers of the former trustee.

Section 7: In all cases described in Section 3, the State Government shall appoint one or more committees in every division or district. Each committee shall consist of three or more persons, appointed from among persons professing the religion for which the establishment was founded, and shall perform all duties previously imposed on the Board of Revenue and local agents, except for property under Section 21.

Section 10: When a vacancy occurs among committee members, a new member shall be elected by interested persons. The remaining committee members must give public notice of the vacancy and fix an election day within three months, under rules framed by the State Government. If the vacancy is not filled by election within three months, the Civil Court may appoint a person or order the remaining members to fill it.

Section 14: Any interested person may sue before the Civil Court the trustee, manager, superintendent, or committee member for any misfeasance, breach of trust, or neglect of duty. The Civil Court may direct specific performance, decree damages and costs, and direct the removal of such trustee, manager, superintendent, or committee member.
administration: The State Government is responsible for making special provisions, transferring property from the Board of Revenue and local agents, and appointing committees for the superintendence and management of religious establishments. The Civil Court has jurisdiction over disputes regarding succession to trusteeship, removal of committee members, filling committee vacancies, and hearing suits for misfeasance, breach of trust, or neglect of duty. Committees, once appointed, manage the affairs of the religious establishments. The Act explicitly divests the Central Government and State Governments from undertaking or resuming superintendence, management, or appointment of trustees for such religious endowments.

title: ACT No.XIV. OF 1852. An Act for extending the provisions of Acts XXIV.of 1841. and XVII. of 1843, to the Straits Settlement.
purpose: To address doubts whether Acts XXIV. of 1841. and XVII. of 1843, are in force in the Settlement of Prince of Wales’ Islands, Singapore and Malacca.
scope: The Settlement of Prince of Wales’ Islands, Singapore and Malacca (Straits Settlement).
key_provisions: Extending Acts 24,1841 and 17,1843 to Straits Settlements.
Extending provisions of above Acts relating to Supreme Court to Court of Judicature of Straits Settlements.
I. The Provisions of Acts XXIV . of 1841, and XVII. of 1843, shall be applicable and in force in the said Settlement.
II. All provisions contained in Act XXIV. of 1841, and Act XVII. of 1843, relating to Her Majesty’s Supreme Courts shall be applicable to the Court of Judicature of the said Settlement.

II. All provisions relating to Her Majesty’s Supreme Courts shall be respectively construed as, if, instead of the words Her Majesty’s Supreme Courts, or Her Majesty’s Supreme Courts of the respective presidencies, or the Supreme Court of each of the Presidencies, the words, “the Court of Judicature of prince of Wales’ Island, Singapore and Malacca,” had been therein mentioned.
administration: information not publicly available

title: The Suits Valuation Act, 1887
purpose: To prescribe the mode of valuing certain suits for the purpose of determining the jurisdiction of Courts with respect thereto.
scope: Extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. Part I extends to such local areas and comes into force on such dates as the State Government directs by notification in the Official Gazette. Part II came into force on the first day of July, 1887.
key_provisions: Section 3(1): The State Government may make rules for determining the value of land for purposes of jurisdiction in the suits mentioned in the Court-fees Act, 1870 (7 of 1870), section 7, paragraphs v and vi, and paragraph x, clause (d).

Section 4: Where a suit mentioned in the Court-fees Act, 1870 (7 of 1870), section 7, paragraph iv, or Schedule II, article 17, relates to land or an interest in land of which the value has been determined by rules under the last foregoing section, the amount at which for purposes of jurisdiction the relief sought in the suit is valued shall not exceed the value of the land or interest as determined by those rules.

Section 5(1) & (2): The State Government shall, before making rules under section 3, consult the High Court with respect thereto. A rule under that section shall not take effect till the expiration of one month after the rule has been published in the Official Gazette.

Section 8: Where in suits other than those referred to in the Court-fees Act, 1870 (7 of 1870), section 7, paragraphs v, vi and ix, and paragraph x, clause (d), court-fees are payable ad valorem under the Court-fees Act, 1870, the value as determinable for the computation of court-fees and the value for purposes of jurisdiction shall be the same.

Section 9: When the subject-matter of suits of any class, other than suits mentioned in the Court-fees Act, 1870 (7 of 1870), section 7, paragraphs v and vi, and paragraph x, clause (d), is such that in the opinion of the High Court it does not admit of being satisfactorily valued, the High Court may, with the previous sanction of the State Government, direct that suits of that class shall, for the purposes of the Court-fees Act, 1870, and of this Act and any other enactment for the time being in force, be treated as if their subject-matter were of such value as the High Court thinks fit to specify in this behalf.

Section 11(1): An objection that by reason of the over-valuation or under-valuation of a suit or appeal a Court of first instance or lower Appellate Court which had not jurisdiction with respect to the suit or appeal exercised jurisdiction with respect thereto shall not be entertained by an Appellate Court unless (a) the objection was taken in the Court of first instance at or before the hearing at which issues were first framed and recorded, or in the lower Appellate Court in the memorandum of appeal to that Court, or (b) the Appellate Court is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded by it in writing, that the suit or appeal was over-valued or under-valued, and that the over-valuation or under-valuation thereof has prejudicially affected the disposal of the suit or appeal on its merits.
administration: The State Government is empowered to make rules for determining the value of land for jurisdictional purposes (Section 3) and to direct the extent and commencement of Part I of the Act by notification in the Official Gazette (Section 2). Before making such rules, the State Government must consult the High Court (Section 5(1)), and rules take effect one month after publication in the Official Gazette (Section 5(2)). The High Court, with the previous sanction of the State Government, may determine the value of certain suits for jurisdictional purposes where satisfactory valuation is not otherwise possible (Section 9). Appellate Courts and Courts exercising revisional jurisdiction are responsible for entertaining objections regarding the proper valuation of suits or appeals for jurisdictional purposes (Section 11).

title: THE PROVINCIAL SMALL CAUSE COURTS ACT, 1887
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to Courts of Small Causes established beyond the local limits for the time being of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the High Courts of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal and at Madras and Bombay.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India except "the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States"; and it came into force on the first day of July, 1887. It applies to Courts of Small Causes established beyond the local limits for the time being of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of a High Court of Judicature established in a Presidency-town.
key_provisions: Establishment of Courts and Appointment of Judges: The State Government may, by order in writing, establish a Court of Small Causes (Section 5(1)). A Judge shall be appointed to each established Court, and the same person may be Judge of more than one Court (Section 6). Additional Judges may also be appointed (Section 8(1)).

Cognizance of Suits: A Court of Small Causes shall not take cognizance of suits specified in the Second Schedule (Section 15(1)). Subject to these exceptions, all suits of a civil nature of which the value does not exceed five hundred rupees shall be cognizable by a Court of Small Causes (Section 15(2)). The State Government may, by order, direct that suits up to one thousand rupees shall be cognizable (Section 15(3)).

Application of the Code of Civil Procedure: The procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), shall be followed in a Court of Small Causes in all cognizable suits and proceedings, unless otherwise provided by that Code or this Act (Section 17(1)). An applicant to set aside an ex parte decree or for review must deposit the amount due or give security as directed by the Court (Section 17(1) Proviso).

Exclusive Jurisdiction: Save as expressly provided by this Act or any other enactment, a suit cognizable by a Court of Small Causes shall not be tried by any other Court having jurisdiction within the local limits of the Court of Small Causes by which the suit is triable (Section 16).

Revision of Decrees and Orders: The High Court, for the purpose of satisfying itself that a decree or order made in any case decided by a Court of Small Causes was according to law, may call for the case and pass such order with respect thereto as it thinks fit (Section 25).

Registrar's Jurisdiction and Duties: The State Government may confer upon a Registrar the jurisdiction of a Judge of a Court of Small Causes for the trial of suits of which the value does not exceed twenty rupees (Section 12(3)). The Registrar shall try such suits and execute decrees passed therein (Section 18(1)). In the absence of a Judge or Additional Judge, the Registrar may admit, return, or reject plaints (Section 19(1)), pass decrees on confession (Section 20(1)), and make orders for execution of decrees (Section 21(1)).
administration: A Court of Small Causes is subject to the administrative control of the District Court and the superintendence of the High Court. It must keep registers, books, and accounts as prescribed by the High Court and comply with requisitions for records, returns, and statements from the District Court, High Court, or State Government. The State Government prescribes the form and dimensions of the Court's seal and may abolish a Court of Small Causes by order in writing. All orders required by this Act to be made in writing by the State Government must be published in the Official Gazette.

title: THE BENGAL, AGRA AND ASSAM CIVIL COURTS ACT, 1887
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to Civil Courts in Bengal, the North-Western Provinces and Assam.
scope: It extends to the territories which were on the 11th March, 1887, respectively administered by the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, the Lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces and the Chief Commissioner of Assam, except such portions of those territories as for the time being are not subject to the ordinary civil jurisdiction of the High Courts.
key_provisions: Section 3: There shall be the following classes of Civil Courts under this Act: the Court of the District Judge, the Court of the Additional Judge, the Court of the Subordinate Judge, and the Court of the Munsif.

Section 18: The jurisdiction of a District Judge or Subordinate Judge extends, subject to the provisions of section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure (14 of 1882), to all original suits for the time being cognizable by Civil Courts.

Section 19: The jurisdiction of a Munsif extends to all like suits of which the value does not exceed one thousand rupees, with the State Government having the power to extend this to two thousand rupees on the recommendation of the High Court.

Section 21: An appeal from a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge shall lie to the District Judge where the value of the original suit did not exceed five thousand rupees, and to the High Court in any other case. An appeal from a decree or order of a Munsif shall lie to the District Judge.

Section 25: The State Government may confer upon any Subordinate Judge or Munsif the jurisdiction of a Judge of a Court of Small Causes under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 (9 of 1887), for the trial of suits up to five hundred rupees for a Subordinate Judge or two hundred and fifty rupees for a Munsif.

Section 37: In any suit or proceeding, questions regarding succession, inheritance, marriage or caste, or any religious usage or institution, shall be decided according to Muhammadan law for Muhammadans and Hindu law for Hindus, unless altered or abolished by legislative enactment.
administration: Administration of Civil Courts under this Act is primarily managed by the State Government, High Court, and District Judges. The State Government is responsible for determining the number of judges, filling vacancies, appointing additional judges, and defining local limits and places of sitting for courts. The High Court exercises superintendence over District Judges, prepares holiday lists, and can authorize specific jurisdictional powers. District Judges hold administrative control over Civil Courts within their local limits, including assigning business and transferring proceedings.

title: THE DEHRA DUN ACT, 1871
purpose: To give validity to the operation of the General Regulations and Acts within the district under the Superintendent of the Dehra Dun.
scope: The Act extends to the district of Dehra Dun, but nothing in this Act shall apply to that portion of the Dehra Dun district called Jaunsar Bawar.
key_provisions: Section 1: The Regulations and Acts now in force in the district of Saharanpur are hereby declared to extend to the said district of Dehra Dun.

Section 2: The High Court and the Board of Revenue of Uttar Pradesh shall exercise, respectively, in the said district, all the powers which the said High Court or Board of Revenue are at present, respectively, authorized to exercise in any part of Agra.
Section 3: The District Court of Saharanpur shall be the District Court of such district until the State Government otherwise directs.
Section 4: Nothing in this Act shall apply to that portion of the Dehra Dun district called Jaunsar Bawar.
administration: The High Court and the Board of Revenue of Uttar Pradesh shall exercise powers in the district as per Section 2. The State Government may direct changes regarding the District Court as per Section 3.

title: THE CHARITABLE ENDOWMENTS ACT, 1890
purpose: To provide for the vesting and administration of property held in trust for charitable purposes.
scope: It extends to the whole of India. 'Charitable purpose' includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship (Section 2).
key_provisions: Section 3: The Central Government may appoint a Treasurer of Charitable Endowments for India, and State Governments may appoint a Treasurer for their respective States. Such treasurer shall be a corporation sole for taking, holding, and transferring property, with perpetual succession and a corporate seal, and may sue and be sued in their corporate name.

Section 4: The appropriate Government may, on application, order by notification in the Official Gazette, that property held or to be applied in trust for charitable purposes be vested in the Treasurer of Charitable Endowments on agreed terms regarding its application or income.

Section 5: The appropriate Government may, on application and with concurrence of the applicants, settle or modify a scheme for the administration of property vested or to be vested in the Treasurer, and may appoint persons (not including the Treasurer) to administer the property. Such schemes supersede repugnant decrees and their validity cannot be questioned in court.

Section 6: Applications for vesting orders (Section 4) and administration schemes (Section 5) must be made by the person(s) acting in the administration of an existing trust (or a majority of them) or by the person(s) proposing to apply property in trust for a charitable purpose.

Section 8: A Treasurer of Charitable Endowments shall not, as such treasurer, act in the administration of any trust. The treasurer shall keep a separate account for each vested property (if securities for money) and apply it according to the vesting order or scheme. For other property, the treasurer shall permit administrators to have possession, management, and control.

Section 13: The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for prescribing fees, regulating the publication of schemes before settlement, prescribing forms for accounts kept by treasurers and their audit mode, and generally for carrying into effect the Act's purposes.
administration: The Act is administered by the 'appropriate Government', which is either the Central Government or a State Government depending on the charitable endowment's scope (Section 3A). The appropriate Government appoints a Treasurer of Charitable Endowments (Section 3), who acts as a corporation sole, holding property and keeping separate accounts for each vested property, but not actively administering the trust (Section 8). The appropriate Government issues orders for vesting property (Section 4) and settles or modifies schemes for its administration (Section 5). The Treasurer is required to publish annually in the Official Gazette a list of all vested properties and an abstract of accounts (Section 9). The appropriate Government also has the power to make rules for the Act's implementation, including prescribing fees, regulating scheme publication, and dictating account forms and audit modes (Section 13). In Karnataka, the State Government may delegate certain powers, except rule-making, to subordinate officers for endowments not exceeding rupees ten thousand, with specific restrictions for powers under sections 4 and 5 (Section 12A).

title: THE COASTING -VESSELS ACT, 1838
purpose: To establish rules for the marking, branding, registration, and certification of vessels belonging to any citizen of India, employed on the coasts or in trading coastwise, as well as fishing-vessels and harbour-craft.
scope: This Act extends in the first instance to the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in the States of Bombay, Saurashtra and Kutch, but the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend it to any other State or part of a State which has a sea-coast. It applies to vessels belonging to any citizen of India and employed on the coasts of any State or part of a State to which this Act extends or in trading coastwise, as well as fishing-vessels and harbour-craft belonging to any such citizen.
key_provisions: Section 3: Every vessel, fishing-vessel, and harbour-craft shall be marked or branded with the name of its place and a number assigned by the authorised officer. The owner must paint this name and number in black paint upon a white ground on each quarter, in English figures and letters, each six inches in length.

Section 4: The name, number, burthen, and owner's name of every vessel, fishing-vessel, and harbour-craft shall be registered in a book. Registry is made by the Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department at Bombay, and by the Commissioner of Customs or a Central Government appointee at other places. Re-registry is required for changes in burthen or ownership, and no new name other than the first registered name is allowed.

Section 5: Owners of vessels, fishing-vessels, and harbour-craft must apply to the authorised person for initial registry or re-registry. If registered at a subordinate port, the registering officer must immediately inform the Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department at Bombay of the registry and assigned number.

Section 7: Owners must apply for and obtain a certificate of registry from the authorised person. The certificate must be in the form specified in the Schedule appended to this Act. A renewed certificate may be obtained in the same manner and on payment of fees if the original is lost or destroyed.

Section 10: Fees for certificates of registry are: 1 rupee for vessels not exceeding 5 tons burthen; 5 rupees for vessels exceeding 5 tons but not exceeding 25 tons burthen; 7 rupees for vessels exceeding 25 tons but not exceeding 100 tons burthen; and 2 annas per ton for vessels of 100 tons or greater burthen.

Section 13: Penalties for non-compliance include: a fine of ten times the certificate fee for vessels (if a fee is payable) or ten rupees for fishing-vessels/harbour-craft, if a vessel is not marked/branded, name/number not painted, not furnished with a certificate, or if the certificate is not produced on demand. Fines may be recovered by sale of the vessel, her furniture, ammunition, tackle, and apparel, and are payable for each subsequent default after one month from the last conviction.
administration: Registry, marking, branding, and ascertaining burthen are performed by the Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department at Bombay, and by the Commissioner of Customs or other persons appointed by the Central Government at other places. The Central Government appoints officers to receive and credit fees, and may direct compensation for seizing vessels. Penalties are recovered on conviction before any Magistrate.

title: THE POWERS-OF-ATTORNEY ACT, 1882
purpose: To amend the law relating to Powers-of-Attorney.
scope: It applies to the whole of India
key_provisions: Section 1A: In this Act, “Power-of-Attorney” includes any instrument empowering a specified person to act for and in the name of the person executing it.

Section 2: The donee of a power-of-attorney may execute or do any instrument or thing in and with his own name and signature, and his own seal, by the authority of the donor, and such act shall be as effectual in law as if done by the donee in the donor's name, signature, and seal.

Section 3: Any person making or doing any payment or act in good faith, in pursuance of a power-of-attorney, shall not be liable if the donor had died, become of unsound mind, or insolvent, or had revoked the power, provided the person making the payment or act was unaware of such facts at the time.

Section 4(a): An instrument creating a power-of-attorney, its execution being verified by affidavit, statutory declaration or other sufficient evidence, may be deposited in the High Court or District Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the instrument may be.

Section 4(b): A separate file of instruments so deposited shall be kept; and any person may search that file, and inspect every instrument so deposited; and a certified copy thereof shall be delivered out to him on request.

Section 5: A married woman of full age shall, by virtue of this Act, have power, as if she were unmarried, by a non-testamentary instrument, to appoint an attorney on her behalf, for the purpose of executing any non-testamentary instrument or doing any other act which she might herself execute or do.
