administration: The High Court may, from time to time, make rules for the purposes of Section 4 (Deposit of original instruments creating powers-of-attorney), and prescribe fees to be taken under clauses (a), (b) and (c) with the concurrence of the State Government.

title: THE BENGAL GHATWALI LANDS ACT, 1859
purpose: To empower the holder of Ghatwalee lands in the District of Beerbhoom to grant leases extending beyond the period of their own possession, for the development of mineral resources and improvement of said lands, as Ghatwals previously lacked the power of alienating their lands.
scope: Applies to Ghatwalee lands in the District of Beerbhoom held by Ghatwals who pay revenue directly to Government under Regulation XXIX. 1814 of the Bengal Code, and also to such lands when under the superintendence of the Court of Wards or direct control of Officers of Government.
key_provisions: Section I: Ghatwals holding lands in the District of Beerbhoom under Regulation XXIX. 1814 shall have the power to grant leases for any period deemed most conducive to the improvement of their tenures, as is allowed by law to the proprietors of other lands.

Proviso to Section I: No lease of Ghatwalee lands extending beyond the grantor's life-time or incumbency shall be valid and binding on successors unless granted for the working of mines, clearing of jungle, erection of dwelling houses or manufactories, or for tanks, canals, and similar works.

Proviso to Section I: Any such lease extending beyond the grantor's life-time or incumbency must be approved by the Commissioner of the Division, with such approval certified by an endorsement on the lease under the Commissioner's signature.

Section II: If Ghatwalee lands are under the superintendence of the Court of Wards or direct control of Officers of Government, the Court of Wards or the Commissioner is lawful to grant leases for the purposes specified in the Act.

Section II: Every lease granted by the Court of Wards or the Commissioner under Section II shall be valid and binding on all future possessors of the said lands, anything in the existing law to the contrary notwithstanding.
administration: The Commissioner of the Division is responsible for approving certain leases. The Court of Wards and the Commissioner are empowered to grant leases for Ghatwalee lands under their superintendence or direct control of Officers of Government.

title: THE BENGAL LAND REVENUE SALES ACT, 1859
purpose: To improve the law relating to sales of Land for arrears of Revenue in the Lower Provinces under the Bengal Presidency, including discontinuing the practice of obtaining previous sanction of the Board of Revenue for sales in Cuttack, securing persons with liens, affording sharers means to protect their shares from co-sharer defaults, guarding landholders against accidental sales, providing for voluntary registration of dependent talooks, and protecting holders of registered under-tenures from loss by avoidance on sale of the superior estate.
scope: The operation of this Act is confined to such parts of the Lower Provinces in the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal as are or shall be subject to the general Regulations of that Presidency, specifically mentioning the Provinces of Bengal, Behar and Orissa.
key_provisions: Section III: The Board of Revenue at Calcutta shall determine and publish the latest dates for payment of revenue arrears and other demands in each district. Notice of these dates must be given in the official Gazette and published in the language of the district in the Office of the Collector, Courts of the Judge, Magistrate, and Moonsiffs, and at every Thannah station. Changes to these dates require advertisement and notification at least three months before the close of the official year preceding the change.

Section IX: The Collector shall, before sunset of the latest payment day, receive as a deposit from any person not being a proprietor the amount of the arrear of revenue due. If the depositor is a party in a suit for possession, the Court may order temporary possession, subject to security rules. A depositor proving the deposit protected an interest may recover the amount from the defaulting proprietor, or if protecting a lien, the amount shall be added to the original lien.

Sections X & XI: A recorded sharer of a joint estate desiring to pay their government revenue separately may submit a written application to the Collector. The Collector shall publish a copy of the application in his Office, Courts, Thannahs, and on the estate. If no objection is made by any other recorded sharer within six weeks from publication, the Collector shall open a separate account with the applicant, with separate liabilities commencing from the sanction date. If an objection is made, the parties are referred to the Civil Court (Section XII).

Section XXXVII: A purchaser of an entire permanently settled estate sold for its own arrears acquires it free from all encumbrances imposed after settlement and is entitled to avoid under-tenures and eject under-tenants, with exceptions for: (1) Istemraree or mokurreree tenures at fixed rent since permanent settlement; (2) Tenures existing at settlement not at fixed rent (rents liable to enhancement); (3) Talookdaree and similar tenures/farms created since settlement and duly registered under this Act; (4) Leases of lands with permanent buildings, gardens, tanks, wells, canals, places of worship, or mines.

Sections XL, XLI, XLII: Holders of talookdaree tenures or farms may apply by petition to the Collector for common or special registry, providing specific particulars (e.g., location, nature, rent, date, names). For common registry, the Collector serves and affixes notices, allowing 30 days for objections. If no objection or if an objection is deemed improbable, the Collector registers. For special registry, similar notice and objection procedures apply, but if no objection, the Collector conducts an inquiry for Government revenue security and reports to the Commissioner, who directs registration if satisfied.

Section XXV: The Commissioner of Revenue may receive an appeal against any sale made under this Act if preferred to him on or before the fifteenth day from the date of sale, or to the Collector for transmission on or before the tenth day. The Commissioner is competent to annul any sale not conducted according to the Act's provisions, awarding compensation for loss if occasioned by proprietor's neglect, with the Commissioner's order being final.
administration: The Act is administered by the Board of Revenue at Calcutta, Collectors (or other officers authorized to hold sales), and Commissioners of Revenue. The Board of Revenue determines payment dates, authorizes specific actions, and reviews annulment recommendations. Collectors are responsible for issuing sale notifications, conducting sales, receiving deposits, managing separate accounts, issuing certificates, and enforcing possession. Commissioners handle appeals against sales, may suspend orders, and direct special registries. Civil Courts have jurisdiction over disputes, annulment of sales, and execution of decrees related to the Act.

title: THE OUDH LAWS ACT, 1876
purpose: To declare and amend the laws to be administered in Oudh.
scope: It extends only to Oudh.
key_provisions: Section 3(b) establishes that in questions regarding succession, special property of female, betrothal, marriage, divorce, dower, adoption, guardianship, minority, bastardy, family relations, wills, legacies, gifts, partitions or any religious usage or institution, the rule of decision shall be any custom applicable to the parties concerned which is not contrary to justice, equity or good conscience, or the Muhammadan law for Muhammadans, and Hindu law for Hindus, unless altered by enactment or modified by custom.

Section 5 dictates that if a Muhammadan dower contract stipulates an excessive amount relative to the husband's means, the Court shall award a reasonable amount with reference to the husband's means and the wife's status, applicable whether the suit is brought in the husband's lifetime or after his death.

Section 10 outlines the procedure for 'Notice to pre-emptors': when any person proposes to sell property or forecloses a mortgage where pre-emption rights exist, notice of the price or amount due must be given through the Court within whose local limits the property is situated, and is deemed sufficiently given if stuck up on the chaupal or other public place of the village or city.

Section 19 repeals Section 172 of Act No. 8 of 1859 for Oudh and substitutes rules for taking evidence: witnesses' evidence shall be taken orally in open Court, a note of essential points taken by the officer trying the case in his own language or English, filed as part of the record, and interpreted to the witness if they do not understand the language of transcription.

Section 20 restricts the 'Execution-sale of ancestral and acquired property in land': ancestral land, defined to include land owned continuously from the first regular settlement, land forming an estate under the Oudh Estates Act, 1869, land conferred as a reward, or the interest of a land revenue grant holder, shall not be sold in satisfaction of a decree without the permission of the State Government.

Section 34 details the 'Duties of village and road police-man': they shall give immediate information to the police-station officer of unnatural/suspicious deaths and specified offences (e.g., murder, dacoity, theft), keep police informed of disputes, arrest proclaimed offenders and those committing specified offences, report movements of bad characters, and supply local information to Magistrates or police officers.
administration: The Act is administered by the Courts of Oudh. Specific powers and rule-making authority are vested in the State Government (e.g., for police appointments, rule-making under Section 39, and permission for ancestral land sales under Section 20), the High Court (for rules regarding custody and sale of attached property under Section 27), and Magistrates of the district (for matters concerning village and road police, including dismissal under Section 36).

title: BENGAL INDIGO CONTRACTS ACT, 1836
purpose: To regulate disputes concerning the right to Indigo Plant, enforce lawful contracts for indigo cultivation and delivery, provide legal recourse for breaches of such contracts, and repeal Clause Third, Section V., Regulation VI., 1823, of the Bengal Code.
scope: This Act applies to contested rights to Indigo Plant, lawful contracts between a ryut and another party for the cultivation or delivery of Indigo Plant, and suits instituted under the provisions of Regulation VI., 1823, of the Bengal Code, or under the provisions of this Act.
key_provisions: Clause Third, Section V., Regulation VI., 1823, of the Bengal Code, is hereby repealed (Section I).

Whenever the right to Indigo Plant is contested and an order is passed under Clause Ninth, Section III., Regulation VI., 1823, for delivery, the party receiving shall not cut or remove the plant until giving sufficient security to the Court trying the case to make good any ultimately established claim (Section II).

If any person, knowing of a lawful indigo contract and advance, prevails upon a ryut to break such contract, the party who made the advance is entitled to proceed by civil action against that person and the ryut, jointly or severally, to recover damages to the extent of injury sustained, together with costs of suit (Section III).

The Court trying any suit instituted under Regulation VI., 1823, or this Act, is authorized to examine both the plaintiff and the defendant when deemed necessary, and if the award favors the defendant, to assign compensation for expense and loss of time (Section IV).

A Zillah or City Judge may refer any suit (regular or summary) instituted under Regulation VI., 1823, or this Act, to a Principal Sudder Ameen or Sudder Ameen for inquiry and decision, according to their respective jurisdictions and rules (Section V).
administration: The administration of this Act involves Courts, specifically the 'Court trying the case' which ensures security in indigo plant disputes (Section II). Civil actions are the mechanism for parties to recover damages for contract breaches (Section III). Courts are authorized to examine parties and assign compensation (Section IV). Zillah or City Judges may refer suits to a Principal Sudder Ameen or Sudder Ameen for inquiry and decision (Section V).

title: THE LEGAL REPRESENTATIVES’ SUITS ACT, 1855
purpose: To enable executors, administrators or representatives in certain cases to sue and be sued in respect of certain wrongs which, according to the present law, do not survive to or against such executors, administrators or representatives.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India, with specific extensions to Dadra and Nagar Haveli, the Union Territory of Pondicherry, the State of Sikkim, and various Scheduled Districts as detailed in the footnotes. It specifically enables actions by and against legal representatives for wrongs committed within one year before the deceased's death that occasioned pecuniary loss to the estate or for which the deceased would have been subject to an action.
key_provisions: Section 1: An action may be maintained by the executors, administrators or representatives of any deceased person for wrongs committed in their lifetime that occasioned pecuniary loss to the estate, provided the wrong was committed within one year before death.

Section 1: An action may be maintained against the executors, administrators, heirs or representatives of any deceased person for wrongs committed by them in their lifetime, provided the wrong was committed within one year before death.
Section 1: Damages recovered by legal representatives shall be part of the personal estate of the deceased.

Section 1: Damages recovered against an executor or administrator (bound to administer according to English law) shall be payable in the same order of administration as the simple contract debts of such person.

Section 2: No action commenced under this Act shall abate by reason of the death of either party, but may be continued by or against the executors, administrators or representatives of the deceased party.
Section 2 Proviso: Executors, administrators, or representatives defending an action may set up a want of assets as a defence, either wholly or in part.
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE TRANSFER OF PROPERTY ACT, 1882
purpose: to define and amend certain parts of the law relating to the transfer of property by act of parties
scope: It extends in the first instance to the whole of India, except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States or in the States of Bombay, Punjab and Delhi. The Act or any part thereof may be extended to these territories by notification in the Official Gazette by the State Government concerned. State Governments may also exempt, retrospectively or prospectively, any part of their administered territories from Sections 54 (paragraphs 2 and 3), 59, 107 and 123. These specific sections shall not extend or be extended to any district or tract of country excluded from the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908.
key_provisions: Section 5: "Transfer of property" defined. "In the following sections “transfer of property” means an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself, and one or more other living persons; and “to transfer property” is to perform such act. “Living person” includes a company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not."

Section 6: What may be transferred. "Property of any kind may be transferred, except as otherwise provided by this Act or by any other law for the time being in force." Specific exceptions include the chance of an heir-apparent, a mere right of re-entry, an easement apart from dominant heritage, an interest restricted to personal enjoyment, a right to future maintenance, a mere right to sue, a public office or its salary, stipends to military/naval/air-force/civil pensioners, and transfers opposed to the nature of interest, for unlawful object/consideration, or to a legally disqualified transferee.

Section 10: Condition restraining alienation. "Where property is transferred subject to a condition or limitation absolutely restraining the transferee or any person claiming under him from parting with or disposing of his interest in the property, the condition or limitation is void, except in the case of a lease where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor or those claiming under him."

Section 14: Rule against perpetuity. "No transfer of property can operate to create an interest which is to take effect after the lifetime of one or more persons living at the date of such transfer, and the minority of some person who shall be in existence at the expiration of that period, and to whom, if he attains full age, the interest created is to belong."

Section 54: “Sale” defined and how made. "“Sale” is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised. For tangible immoveable property of value one hundred rupees and upwards, or reversion/intangible thing, sale can be made only by a registered instrument. For tangible immoveable property of value less than one hundred rupees, sale may be made by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property."

Section 58: Types of Mortgages defined. "A mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific immoveable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability." The Act defines Simple mortgage, Mortgage by conditional sale, Usufructuary mortgage, English mortgage, Mortgage by deposit of title-deeds (applicable in Calcutta, Madras, Bombay, and other specified towns), and Anomalous mortgage.
administration: The Act is administered through the courts for dispute resolution and enforcement. State Governments have the power to extend the Act or parts thereof to certain territories by notification in the Official Gazette, and to exempt territories from specific provisions (Sections 54, paragraphs 2 and 3, 59, 107 and 123). For matters concerning incumbrances and sales, 'Court' includes High Courts, District Judges' Courts, and other courts declared competent by the State Government via Official Gazette notification. Courts are also involved in the appointment of receivers under Section 69A if parties fail to agree.

title: THE SOCIETIES REGISTRATION ACT, 1860
purpose: for improving the legal condition of societies established for the promotion of literature, science, or the fine arts, or for the diffusion of useful knowledge, the diffusion of political education or for charitable purposes
scope: Charitable societies, the military orphan funds or societies established at the several presidencies of India, societies established for the promotion of science, literature, or the fine arts, for instruction, the diffusion of useful knowledge, the diffusion of political education, the foundation or maintenance of libraries or reading-rooms for general use among the members or open to the public, or public museums and galleries of paintings and other works of art, collections of natural history, mechanical and philosophical inventions, instruments, or designs.
key_provisions: Section 1: Any seven or more persons associated for any literary, scientific, or charitable purpose, or for any such purpose as is described in section 20 of this Act, may, by subscribing their names to a memorandum of association, and filing the same with the Registrar of Joint-stock Companies, form themselves into a society under this Act.

Section 3: Upon such memorandum and certified copy being filed, the Registrar shall certify under his hand that the society is registered under this Act. There shall be paid to the Registrar for every such registration fee of fifty rupees, or such smaller fee as the State Government may, from time to time, direct.

Section 4: Once in every year, on or before the fourteenth day succeeding the day on which, according to the rules of the society, the annual general meeting of the society is held, or, if the rules do not provide for an annual general meeting, in the month of January, a list shall be filed with the Registrar of Joint-stock Companies, of the names, addresses and occupations of the governors, council, directors, committee, or other governing body then entrusted with the management of the affairs of the society.

Section 12: The governing body of any society may alter, extend, or abridge its purposes or amalgamate with another society by submitting a proposition to members in a written or printed report, convening a special meeting (with 10 days' notice), and securing agreement by votes of three-fifths of members (in person or by proxy) at that meeting, confirmed by votes of three-fifths of members present at a second special meeting convened one month after the former meeting.

Section 13: Any number not less than three-fifths of the members of any society may determine that it shall be dissolved, and all necessary steps shall be taken for the disposal and settlement of the property, claims, and liabilities. In the event of any dispute, the adjustment of its affairs shall be referred to the principal Court of original civil jurisdiction of the district in which the chief building of the society is situate.

Section 12C (Union territory of Ladakh Reorganisation (Adaptation of Central Laws) Second Order, 2020): Every governing body entrusted with the management of the affairs of a society shall keep regular accounts in such form as may be approved by the Registrar, balanced each year on the 31st day of March or such other day as may be fixed by the Registrar, and audited annually by a Chartered Accountant or such persons as may be authorised in this behalf by the Administration of the Union territory of Ladakh.
administration: The Act is administered by a Registrar of Societies (originally Registrar of Joint-stock Companies), appointed by the State Government or the Administration of a Union territory by notification. The Registrar exercises powers and performs duties conferred by the Act and superintends its administration. The State Government or Administration may also appoint one or more Additional Registrars with local jurisdiction, who shall exercise powers and functions subject to the control of the Registrar of Societies.

title: THE STAGE -CARRIAGES ACT, 1861
purpose: To license and regulate stage-carriages.
scope: This Act applies to every carriage drawn by one or more horses (or other animals) ordinarily used for conveying passengers for hire to or from any place in the States. It extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. It does not apply to carriages ordinarily plying for hire within the limits of any municipality or cantonment or other place where a local law for the regulation of carriages is in force. The State Government may exempt any carriages or class of carriages from all or any provisions of this Act by notification in the Official Gazette.
key_provisions: Section 2 & 3: No carriage shall be used as a stage-carriage unless licensed by a Magistrate or Commissioner of Police. The licensing authority may refuse a license if the carriage is unserviceable, unsafe, or unfit for public accommodation. If granted, the license shall set forth its number, proprietor's name and residence, head office location, maximum passengers and luggage weight, number of horses, and place of licensing.

Section 4: A sum of five rupees or a lesser amount fixed by the State Government shall be paid for each license, which is valid for one year. If a licensed stage-carriage is transferred, the new proprietor's name shall be substituted in the license without further payment for that year upon application.

Section 5 & 6: The proprietor of a licensed stage-carriage must cause the license number and all other particulars to be distinctly painted in English on a conspicuous part of the carriage. Failure to do so before letting the carriage for hire incurs a fine not exceeding one hundred rupees.

Section 8: Any proprietor, agent, or driver of a licensed stage-carriage who knowingly permits it to be drawn by fewer horses, or to carry more passengers or luggage than specified by the license, is liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred rupees for a first conviction, and up to five hundred rupees for subsequent convictions.

Section 10: Any Magistrate or Commissioner of Police within whose jurisdiction a stage-carriage plies, or who granted its license, may cancel the license if the stage-carriage, or any horse or harness used with it, is unserviceable, unsafe, or otherwise unfit for public accommodation or use.

Section 20A: The State Government may make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out the Act's purposes, including prescribing license forms, fees, conditions for grant and revocation, providing for inspection of carriages and animals, and regulating the number and length of stages for animals. Breach of such rules may be punishable with a fine up to one hundred rupees.
administration: The Act is administered by Magistrates (including all persons exercising the powers of a Magistrate), Commissioners of Police of Presidency-towns, State Governments, and police officers. Magistrates and Commissioners of Police are responsible for licensing, refusing and revoking licenses, adjudicating penalties, and issuing summons. State Governments are empowered to fix license fees, make rules, and grant exemptions. Police officers may seize carriages for non-compliance with display requirements.

title: THE INDIAN EASEMENTS ACT, 1882
purpose: to define and amend the law relating to Easements and Licenses
scope: The Act extends to the territories respectively administered by the Governor of Madras in Council and the Chief Commissioners of the Central Provinces and Coorg, with the local extent for the State of Karnataka being "the whole of the State of Karnataka" as per Karnataka Act 33 of 1978, s. 6. It came into force on the first day of July, 1882.
key_provisions: Section 4: An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own.

Section 15: The right to access and use of light or air, support, or other easements shall be absolute where it has been peaceably enjoyed, as an easement, without interruption, for twenty years. For property belonging to Government, this period is thirty years.

Section 33: The owner of any interest in the dominant heritage, or the occupier, may institute a suit for compensation for the disturbance of an easement or accessory right, provided the disturbance has caused substantial damage to the plaintiff.

Section 47: A continuous easement is extinguished when it totally ceases to be enjoyed as such for an unbroken period of twenty years. A discontinuous easement is extinguished when, for a like period, it has not been enjoyed as such.

Section 52: A license is a right granted by one person to another to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would otherwise be unlawful, and which does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property.

Section 60: A license may be revoked by the grantor, unless it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force, or the licensee, acting upon the license, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution.
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE FATAL ACCIDENTS ACT, 1855
purpose: To provide compensation to families for loss occasioned by the death of a person caused by actionable wrong, making the wrong-doer answerable in damages for the injury so caused.
scope: Extends to the whole of India.
key_provisions: Section 1A: Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages. Every such action or suit shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the deceased, and shall be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator or representative of the person deceased.
Section 2: Not more than one action or suit shall be brought for, and in respect of the same subject-matter of complaint.

Section 2 (Proviso): In any such action or suit, the executor, administrator or representative of the deceased may insert a claim for, and recover any pecuniary loss to the estate of the deceased occasioned by such wrongful act, neglect or default, which sum, when recovered, shall be deemed part of the assets of the estate of the deceased.

Section 3: The plaint in any such action or suit shall give a full particular of the person or persons for the whom, or on whose behalf, such action or suit shall be brought, and of the nature of the claim in respect of which damages shall be sought to be recovered.

Section 4: Interpretation clause defines 'person' to apply to bodies politic and corporate; 'parent' to include father, mother, grand-father, and grand-mother; and 'child' to include son, daughter, grand-son, grand-daughter, step-son, and step-daughter.
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE MADRAS CIVIL COURTS’ ACT, 1873
purpose: to consolidate and amend the law relating to the Civil Courts of the Madras Presidency subordinate to the High Court
scope: It extends to all the territories for the time being under the government of the Governor of Fort. St. George in Council, except the Tracts respectively under the jurisdiction of the Agents for Ganjam and Vizagapatam; and relates to the Civil Courts of the Madras Presidency subordinate to the High Court.
key_provisions: Section 3 & 4: The number of District Courts, Subordinate Judges, and District Munsifs shall be fixed and may be altered by the Local Government, provided that no increase shall be made without the previous sanction of the Governor General in Council.

Section 12: The jurisdiction of a District Munsif extends to all original suits and proceedings of a civil nature, not otherwise exempted, of which the amount or value of the subject-matter does not exceed two thousand five hundred rupees.

Section 13: Appeals from decrees and orders of Subordinate Judges and District Munsifs shall lie to the District Court, except when the amount or value of the subject-matter of the suit exceeds rupees five thousand, in which case the appeal shall lie to the High Court.

Section 16: In suits or proceedings requiring decision on succession, inheritance, marriage, caste, religious usage or institution, the Muhammadan law (for Muhammadans), Hindu law (for Hindus), or any custom having force of law shall be the rule of decision, unless altered or abolished by legislative enactment. In absence of specific rules, the Court shall act according to justice, equity and good conscience.

Section 17: No District Judge, Subordinate Judge or District Munsif shall try any suit in which he is a party or personally interested, or adjudicate on connected proceedings, nor try appeals against decrees or orders passed by himself in another capacity. Such cases must be reported to the immediately subordinate Court for disposal as prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, section six.

Section 20: The High Court may suspend any District Munsif for alleged misconduct or appoint a commission for inquiry, applying the provisions of Act No. XXXVII of 1850. Upon receiving the inquiry report, the High Court may remove, suspend, or reduce the Munsif to a lower grade.
administration: The administration of the Act is primarily vested in the Local Government, the High Court, and District Judges. The Local Government is responsible for fixing and altering the number and locality of District Courts, Subordinate Judges, and District Munsifs (subject to sanction for increases), appointing District and Subordinate Judges, and suspending or removing judges for misconduct. The High Court appoints District Munsifs, fixes their local jurisdiction, may suspend Subordinate Judges and District Munsifs, and holds general control over Civil Courts. District Judges control Civil Courts within their district, assign jurisdiction to Subordinate Judges, manage appeals, and may suspend District Munsifs under their control.

title: THE PRESIDENCY SMALL CAUSE COURTS ACT, 1882
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to the Courts of Small Causes established in the towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay.
scope: This Act applies to the Courts of Small Causes established in the towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (Section 4, 5). The local limits of jurisdiction for each Small Cause Court are the local limits of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the respective High Court (Section 17). Chapter VIII, concerning distresses, extends to every place within the local limits of the ordinary original civil jurisdictions of the High Courts of Judicature at Fort William, Madras and Bombay (Section 50).
key_provisions: Courts of Small Causes are established in each of the towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (Section 5) and are deemed to be Courts subject to the superintendence of the High Court of Judicature at Fort William, Madras or Bombay (Section 6).

The Small Cause Court has jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature where the amount or value of the subject-matter does not exceed two thousand rupees, provided the cause of action has arisen or defendants reside/work within local limits, and leave of the Court may be required (Section 18). The Court has no jurisdiction in certain specified suits, including those concerning revenue, immovable property, or specific performance (Section 19).

Where a suit has been contested, the Small Cause Court may, on the application of either party made within eight days from the date of the decree or order, order a new trial to be held, or alter, set aside or reverse the decree or order (Section 38).

When a person occupies immovable property within the Court's jurisdiction (annual value not exceeding two thousand rupees) as a tenant or by permission, and such tenancy or permission has determined or been withdrawn, and the occupant refuses to deliver up the property, the applicant may apply to the Small Cause Court for a summons against the occupant (Section 41). If the occupant does not appear or show cause, an order for possession may be issued (Section 43).

Any person claiming to be entitled to arrears of rent of any house or premises may apply to any Judge or the Registrar of the Small Cause Court for a distress-warrant (Section 53). The application must be supported by an affidavit or affirmation to the effect of Form A in the Third Schedule. The Judge or Registrar may then issue a warrant under his hand and seal, returnable within six days, to the effect of Form B in the Third Schedule, addressed to a bailiff (Section 54). The bailiff shall seize movable property, make an inventory, and give notice in writing to the effect of Form C in the Third Schedule (Section 59).

If two or more Judges of the Small Cause Court sitting together differ on any question of law or usage having the force of law or the construction of a document, or if in any suit or proceeding where the amount or value of the subject-matter exceeds five hundred rupees, such a question arises upon which the Court entertains reasonable doubt and either party so requires, the Small Cause Court shall draw up a statement of the facts and the point of difference/doubt, and refer such statement with its own opinion for the opinion of the High Court (Section 69).
administration: The Courts of Small Causes are established in Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay (Section 5). They are subject to the superintendence of the respective High Courts (Section 6). A Chief Judge and other Judges are appointed by the State Government (Section 7). The Chief Judge distributes the business of the Court (Section 10). A Registrar and other ministerial officers are appointed, with the Registrar being the chief ministerial officer, and they exercise powers and discharge duties as directed by the Chief Judge (Section 13). The High Court may prescribe the procedure and practice of the Small Cause Court by rules (Section 9). The State Government prescribes the form and dimensions of the Court's seal (Section 12) and approves the list of holidays and vacations (Section 92).

title: THE KING OF OUDH’S ESTATE ACT, 1887
purpose: To provide for the Administration of the Estate of His late Majesty the King of Oudh, otherwise than under the authority of the Civil Courts, as His late Majesty Wajid Ali Shah was exempt from their jurisdiction during his lifetime.
scope: The Act applies to the administration of the property of whatever nature left by His late Majesty the King of Oudh, Wajid Ali Shah, including the settlement and satisfaction of claims against the estate and the distribution of remaining property among his family and dependents. It also covers acts done by the Agent to the Governor General and persons acting under his order in connection with the estate's preservation and administration.
key_provisions: Section 1(1): The Governor General in Council shall have exclusive authority to act in the administration of the property of whatever nature left by His late Majesty the King of Oudh in regard to the settlement and satisfaction of claims against the estate, and may make distribution of the remaining property or its proceeds among the family and dependents.
Section 1(2): No act of the Governor General in Council in connection with the administration or distribution of the property left by His late Majesty shall be liable to be questioned in any Court.

Section 2: The Agent to the Governor General with His late Majesty, and all persons acting under his order, are indemnified and discharged from liability for all acts done since September 20, 1887, in connection with the preservation and administration of the estate, and no suit shall be instituted against them or the Secretary of State for India in Council for these acts.

Section 3: This Act shall take effect notwithstanding any testamentary or other disposition made by His late Majesty, and notwithstanding any proceedings instituted before any Civil Court for administering his estate or collecting debts due to it.

Section 3: Any person who, under any probate, has received or realised any portion of the estate of His late Majesty shall be bound to account therefor to such officer as the Governor General in Council may appoint in this behalf.
administration: The Governor General in Council has exclusive authority for the administration of the estate, including the settlement of claims and distribution of property. The Governor General in Council may also appoint an officer for persons to account to regarding portions of the estate received.

title: THE IMPROVEMENTS IN TOWNS ACT, 1850 (ACT NO. XXVI OF 1850)
purpose: To enable improvements to be made in Towns, by amending Act X. 1842 which proved ineffectual, and to extend like powers to the inhabitants of Towns in the Presidencies under the Government of the East India Company for purposes connected with public health and convenience.
scope: This Act may be put in force by order of the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, within any Town or Suburb (not within the Town of Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay) in any Presidency or Place within the Territories under the Government of the East India Company, where the inhabitants are desirous of making better provision for specific purposes such as making, repairing, cleaning, lighting, or watching public streets, roads, drains, or tanks, or for the prevention of nuisances, or for improving the Town or Suburb in any other manner.
key_provisions: Section II: The Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, may order this Act to be put in force within any Town or Suburb (not within Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay) if inhabitants desire better provision for public streets, roads, drains, tanks, nuisance prevention, or general improvement.

Sections III & IV: An application to put the Act in force requires notice in the Government Gazette and by proclamation, allowing inhabitants to declare their wishes. The Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, shall consider these declarations and issue a final order, published in the Gazette and by proclamation, specifying the purposes for which the Act will be in force.

Section VI: When the Act comes into force, the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, shall appoint the Magistrate and inhabitants as Commissioners to prepare Rules for accomplishing the Act's purposes. These Rules, once approved, have the same force as if inserted in the Act.

Section VII.2: The Rules prepared by Commissioners must define persons/property to be taxed (by House Assessment or Town Duties), the amount/rate of taxes, the manner of raising and collecting them, and ensuring their safety and due application.

Section X: The powers of Act II. 1839, for the recovery of fines, shall be applied by every Magistrate for the recovery of all arrears of taxes and penalties under this Act, whenever required by the Commissioners or their deputed Officers.

Section XIII: All Commissioners must annually, on or before the last day of April, submit to the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, an account of all works executed and sums received and spent in the foregoing year, in such form and with such vouchers as ordered.
administration: The Act is administered by the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, of any Presidency or Place within the Territories under the Government of the East India Company. They are responsible for ordering the Act into force, approving rules, and receiving annual accounts. They appoint Commissioners (comprising the Magistrate and inhabitants) to put the Act in force, prepare rules, make contracts, apply taxes, and manage other expenses incident to the Act's execution.

title: THE BENGAL MILITARY POLICE ACT, 1892
purpose: An Act for the Regulation of the Bengal Military Police; to make provision for the better regulation of the Bengal Reserve Police.
scope: It extends to the whole of the territories subject to the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal.
key_provisions: Section 3 & Schedule: Enrolment of a Military Police-officer requires the statement in the schedule to be read and explained in the presence of a Magistrate, Commandant or Second-in-Command, and signed by the officer. Discharge from service, after three years, requires an application through a subordinate officer to a Commandant or District Magistrate, granted after two months unless vacancies exceed one-tenth of sanctioned strength. No claim to discharge while on active service.

Section 5: A Military Police-officer committing more heinous offences (e.g., mutiny, using criminal force to a superior officer, desertion while on active service, plundering) shall be punished with transportation for life or for a term of not less than seven years, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to fourteen years, or with fine which may extend to three months’ pay, or with fine in addition to transportation or imprisonment.

Section 6: A Military Police-officer committing less heinous offences (e.g., intoxication on duty, striking a sentry, insubordination, injuring equipment, malingering) shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to three months' pay, or with both.

Section 7: A District Magistrate, Commandant, Second-in-Command, or an officer not below the rank of subadar commanding a separate detachment/outpost or in temporary command at headquarters, may, without formal trial, award minor punishments for petty offences against discipline, including imprisonment up to seven days in quarter-guard with forfeiture of pay, or punishment drill/extra duty not exceeding thirty days.

Section 10: The Local Government may invest any Police-officer not below the rank of Commandant with the powers of Magistrate of any class for the purpose of enquiring into or trying any offence committed by a Military Police-officer and punishable under Act V of 1861 or this Act.
Section 13: The Local Government may, as regards the Military Police, make such orders and rules consistent with this Act as it thinks expedient.
administration: The Local Government is responsible for appointing Commandants and Seconds-in-Command, setting the Act's commencement date, directing classes and grades of Military Police-officers, directing places of imprisonment, investing Police-officers with magisterial powers, and making orders and rules consistent with the Act.

title: THE INDIAN TRUSTS ACT, 1882
purpose: To define and amend the law relating to private trusts and trustees.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, with the Central Government having the power to extend it to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands or any part thereof by notification in the Official Gazette. It does not affect the rules of Muhammadan law as to waqf, the mutual relations of members of an undivided family as determined by customary or personal law, or apply to public or private religious or charitable endowments, or to trusts to distribute prizes taken in war among captors. Chapter II of the Act does not apply to trusts created before March 1, 1882.
key_provisions: Section 4: A trust may be created for any lawful purpose. A purpose is unlawful if it is (a) forbidden by law, or (b) is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law, or (c) is fraudulent, or (d) involves or implies injury to the person or property of another, or (e) the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy. Every trust with an unlawful purpose is void.

Section 5: No trust in relation to immoveable property is valid unless declared by a non-testamentary instrument in writing signed by the author of the trust or the trustee and registered, or by the will of the author of the trust or of the trustee. For moveable property, it must be declared as aforesaid, or the ownership of the property must be transferred to the trustee.

Section 11: The trustee is bound to fulfil the purpose of the trust and obey the directions of the author of the trust given at the time of its creation, unless modified by the consent of all competent beneficiaries. If a beneficiary is incompetent to contract, their consent may be given by a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction. A trustee is not required to obey directions that are impracticable, illegal, or manifestly injurious to the beneficiaries.

Section 20: Where trust-property consists of money not immediately applicable, the trustee shall invest it in securities expressly authorised by the instrument of trust or specified by the Central Government via Official Gazette notification. If a person competent to contract is entitled to the income for life or a greater estate, their written consent is required for such investment.

Section 23: A trustee who commits a breach of trust is liable to make good the sustained loss, unless the beneficiary induced the breach by fraud, or, being competent to contract, concurred in or acquiesced in the breach with full knowledge of facts and rights, without coercion or undue influence.

Section 74: If a trustee vacancy or disqualification occurs and it is impracticable to appoint a new trustee under section 73, the beneficiary may apply by petition to a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction for the appointment of a trustee or a new trustee, and the Court may appoint one accordingly. The Court, in appointing new trustees, shall consider the author's wishes, the wishes of any person empowered to appoint, whether the appointment promotes or impedes trust execution, and the interests of all beneficiaries.
administration: The Act is administered through various mechanisms involving the Central Government, State Government, and principal Civil Courts of original jurisdiction. The Central Government may extend the Act's local extent and specifies securities for trust-money investment (Section 1, 20). The State Government directs how trust-property is held when a beneficiary's interest is forfeited (Section 29). Principal Civil Courts of original jurisdiction are involved in granting permissions (e.g., for minors to create trusts (Section 7), for trustees to renounce (Section 46), for applying property of minors for maintenance from capital (Section 41)), controlling discretionary powers (Section 49), authorizing extensions of sale time (Section 22), appointing new trustees (Section 74), discharging trustees (Section 72), and providing opinions, advice, or directions on trust management (Section 34).

title: An Act for appointing a Commissioner of Revenue at Madras.
purpose: To empower the Governor of Fort St. George in Council to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue, to perform in any of the Districts of that Presidency all or any of the duties which, by the General Regulations and Laws of the Presidency, belong to the Board of Revenue collectively.
scope: This Act applies to any of the Districts of the Presidency of Fort St. George and concerns all or any of the duties which, by the General Regulations and Laws of the Presidency, belong to the Board of Revenue collectively, and all things concerning the Revenue of the Districts included in a Commissioner's remit.
key_provisions: I. The Governor of Fort St. George in Council may, from time to time, whenever he shall see fit, depute a member of the Board of Revenue to perform alone, in any of the Districts of that Presidency, all or any of the duties which, by the General Regulations and Laws of the Presidency, belong to the Board of Revenue collectively.

II. When a special Commission shall be given to a Member of the Board of Revenue under this Act, the Member of the Board named therein shall, by virtue thereof, be empowered to exercise, within the limits of his Commission, all the powers and duties which by Law are vested in the Board of Revenue collectively, without exception, or subject to any exceptions or restrictions, which shall be prescribed in such Commission.

III. Every such Commission shall be published in the Fort St. George Gazette, and the Commissioner shall enter on his Office from the date of such publication; and in like manner the revocation or other determination of any such Commission shall be published in the Fort St. George Gazette.

IV. The correspondence and other documents belonging to any such Commission shall be deposited on the determination thereof, in the Office of the Board of Revenue, and shall be deemed records of the said Board.
administration: The Governor of Fort St. George in Council is empowered to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue. Commissions and their revocations or determinations are to be published in the Fort St. George Gazette. Correspondence and other documents belonging to any such Commission are to be deposited in the Office of the Board of Revenue upon its determination.

title: THE KAZIS ACT, 1880
purpose: An Act for the appointment of persons to the Office of Kazi.
scope: It extends, in the first instance, only to the territories administered by the Governor of Fort Saint George in Council. But the Government of any other State may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend it to the whole or any part of the territories under its administration.
key_provisions: Section 1: The Act extends, in the first instance, only to the territories administered by the Governor of Fort Saint George in Council, but the Government of any other State may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend it to the whole or any part of the territories under its administration.

Section 2: The State Government may, if it thinks fit, after consulting the principal Muhammadan residents of such local area, select one or more fit persons and appoint him or them to be Kazis for such local area, if a considerable number of Muhammadans resident in that area desire it.

Section 2: The State Government may suspend or remove any Kazi appointed under this section for misconduct, continuous absence for six months, leaving the local area to reside elsewhere, being declared an insolvent, desiring to be discharged, refusing, or becoming unfit or personally incapable to discharge duties.

Section 3: Any Kazi appointed under this Act may appoint one or more persons as his Naib or Naibs to act in his place in all or any of the matters appertaining to his office throughout the whole or in any portion of the local area for which he is appointed, and may suspend or remove any naib so appointed.
Section 4(a): Nothing in this Act, and no appointment made hereunder, shall be deemed to confer any judicial or administrative powers on any Kazi or Naib Kazi appointed hereunder.

Section 4(b): Nothing in this Act, and no appointment made hereunder, shall be deemed to render the presence of a Kazi or Naib Kazi necessary at the celebration of any marriage or the performance of any rite or ceremony.
administration: The State Government is empowered to appoint, suspend, or remove Kazis (Section 2). Any Kazi appointed under the Act may appoint, suspend, or remove Naib Kazis (Section 3).

title: EASEMENTS (EXTENDING ACT V OF 1882)
purpose: An Act to extend the Indian Easements Act, 1882, to certain areas in which that Act is not in force.
scope: The territories administered by the Governor of Bombay in Council, the lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces and Chief Commissioner of Oudh, and subsequently the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Union territory of Ladakh.
key_provisions: Section 1 extends the Indian Easements Act, 1882 (V of 1882).
Section 1 extends the Act to territories administered by the Governor of Bombay in Council.
Section 1 extends the Act to territories administered by the lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces and Chief Commissioner of Oudh.
Act 8 of 1891 was extended to Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Union territory of Ladakh by Act 34 of 2019, s. 95 and the fifth schedule (w.e.f. 31-10-2019).
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE GOVERNMENT SAVINGS PROMOTION ACT, 1873
purpose: An Act to regulate and channelise the savings from general public into Government Savings Schemes.
scope: It extends to the whole of India.
key_provisions: Section 3A: The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, frame new Savings Schemes or amend or discontinue existing Savings Schemes to promote household savings in the country.
Section 3B(1): A minor who has attained the age of ten years may open and operate an account in the Government Savings Bank, if so permitted under a Savings Scheme.

Section 4(1): Depositors shall designate one or more individuals as nominee(s) to receive the sum due upon the depositor's death, as specified at the time of nomination. If the depositor is a minor or of unsound mind, the nominee shall be designated by the guardian.

Section 4A(4)(a): If a depositor dies without a nomination in force and no probate, letters of administration, or succession certificate is produced within three months, the Authorised Officer may pay the deposit (if it does not exceed such limit as may be prescribed) to any person appearing entitled to receive it or administer the estate of the deceased in accordance with such procedure as may be prescribed.
Section 12A: Any depositor who suffers from physical infirmity, including blindness, may operate and make a deposit through any literate individual whom he authorises.

Section 14A: The amount standing to the credit of any depositor in the Public Provident Fund Scheme shall not be liable to attachment under any decree or order of any court in respect of any debt or liability incurred by the depositor.
administration: The Central Government is responsible for framing new Savings Schemes, amending or discontinuing existing ones (Section 3A), calling for information (Section 7A), and making rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act (Section 15). The day-to-day administration, including handling deposits, payments, and verification, is carried out by 'Authorised Officers' of 'Government Savings Banks' (Section 3(c), 3(g), 4A, 6, 7, 12).

title: THE DEKKHAN AGRICULTURISTS ’ RELIEF ACT, 1879
purpose: To relieve the agricultural classes in certain parts of the Dekkhan from indebtedness.
scope: Sections 1, 11, 56, 60 and 62 extend to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. The rest of this Act extends only to the districts of Poona, Satara, Sholapur and Ahmednagar, but may be extended wholly or in part by the State Government to any other district or districts in the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in the State of Bombay, or to any part or parts of any other such district or districts.
key_provisions: Section 11: Agriculturists to be sued where they reside. Every suit for the recovery of money (as described in Section 3, clause (w)) may, if the defendant or one of several defendants is an agriculturist, be instituted and tried in a Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction such defendant resides, and not elsewhere. This does not affect sections 22 to 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Section 56: Instruments executed by agriculturist not to be deemed valid unless executed before a Village-registrar. No instrument creating, modifying, transferring, evidencing, or extinguishing an obligation for money payment or a charge on property, or being a conveyance or lease, executed by an agriculturist after this Act comes into force, shall be admitted in evidence or acted upon unless it is written by, or under the superintendence of, and attested by, a Village-registrar. This does not apply to criminal proceedings, instruments executed by an agriculturist merely as a surety, or instruments requiring registration under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, 1877.

Section 60: Registration under this Act to be deemed equivalent to registration under Indian Registration Act, 1877. Every instrument executed and registered in accordance with the provisions of this Act shall be deemed duly registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1877. No instrument that should have been executed before a Village-registrar but was otherwise executed shall be registered or authenticated by any officer or public office under the said Act.

Section 62: Exemption of instruments to which the Government or any officer of the Government is a party. Nothing in this Act requires any instrument, to which the Government or any officer of the Government in an official capacity is a party, to be executed before a Village-registrar.
administration: The Act involves the appointment of a 'Village-registrar' for local areas, who is responsible for writing, superintending, and attesting certain instruments executed by agriculturists (Section 56). The State Government has the power to extend the Act to other districts (Section 1).

title: THE BIRTHS, DEATHS AND MARRIAGES REGISTRATION ACT, 1886
purpose: To provide for the voluntary registration of certain births and deaths, for the establishment of General Registry Offices for keeping registers of certain births, deaths and marriages, and for the more effectual registration of those births and deaths and of marriages registered under Act 3 of 1872, the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, and the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1865. It also aims to provide for the authentication and custody of certain existing registers made otherwise than in performance of a duty specially enjoined by law, and to declare copies of entries in those registers admissible in evidence.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. It initially applies to members of every race, sect or tribe to which the Indian Succession Act, 1865 applies (and for which an order under section 332 of that Act is not in force), and all persons professing the Christian religion. The State Government may extend its operation to any other class of persons or local area by notification in the Official Gazette.
key_provisions: **Establishment of General Registry Offices and Appointment of Registrars General (Section 6)**: Each State Government shall establish a general registry office for keeping certified copies of registers of births, deaths, and marriages (registered under this Act or specified marriage Acts) and may appoint a Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages to charge of that office.

**Duty of Registrar to Register Births and Deaths (Section 19)**: Every Registrar of Births and Deaths shall forthwith make an entry of a birth or death in the proper register book if notice is given within the prescribed time and mode by an authorized person, unless there is reason to believe the notice is false (requiring a District Court order) or for an illegitimate child's father without joint request from mother and acknowledging father.

**Persons Authorized to Give Notice of Birth or Death (Sections 20 & 21)**: Notice of birth may be given by the child's father or mother, any person present at the birth, any person occupying the house with knowledge of the birth, any medical practitioner in attendance after birth with personal knowledge, or any person having charge of the child. Notice of death may be given by any relative with knowledge, any person present at the death, any person occupying the house with knowledge of the death, any person in attendance during the last illness, or any person who has seen the body after death.

**Correction of Entry in Register of Births or Deaths (Section 28)**: A Registrar of Births and Deaths may correct an erroneous entry in form or substance in a register kept by him, by an entry in the margin (without altering the original entry), signing and dating the correction, subject to rules made by the State Government. If a certified copy was sent to the Registrar General, a separate certified copy of the original erroneous entry and marginal correction must be sent.

**Appointment and Duties of Commissioners for Existing Registers (Sections 33 & 34)**: The State Government may appoint Commissioners to examine registers or records of births, baptisms, namings, dedications, deaths, burials, or marriages sent to the Registrar General under Section 32. These Commissioners shall inquire into the state, custody, and authenticity of such records and deliver descriptive lists of accurate and faithful registers or records to the Registrar General, certifying them in writing.

**Rule-Making Power (Section 36)**: The State Government may make rules to carry out the purpose of this Act, including fixing fees, prescribing forms, specifying notice times and modes, evidence of identity, register keeping and reporting formats for Registrars, conditions for correcting entries, particulars for Commissioners' descriptive lists, and custody of registers or records.
administration: The administration of the Act primarily involves the State Government, which establishes general registry offices, appoints Registrars General and Registrars of Births and Deaths, supplies register books, makes rules for registration, error correction, and the overall purpose of the Act, and appoints Commissioners for existing registers. The Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages is appointed by the State Government to charge general registry offices, keep indexes, certify copies, superintend Registrars, and receive certified copies and descriptive lists. Registrars of Births and Deaths are appointed by the State Government for local areas or classes of persons, maintain offices, register births and deaths upon notice, grant certificates, send certified copies to the Registrar General, allow searches, and correct errors. Commissioners are appointed by the State Government to examine and authenticate certain existing registers or records.

title: THE INDIAN TOLLS ACT, 1851
purpose: An Act for enabling Government to levy Tolls on Public Roads and Bridges.
scope: This Act extends to the territories administered on the fourth of July, eighteen hundred and fifty-one, by the Governor of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal, the Lieutenant-Governor of North-Western Provinces of Bengal and the Governor of the Presidency of Fort St. George in Council.
key_provisions: Section 2: The State Government may cause such rates of toll to be levied upon any road or bridge which has been, or shall hereafter be, made or repaired at the expense of the Central or any State Government; and may place the collection of such tolls under the management of such persons as may appear to it proper.

Section 3 (Toll Recovery Procedure): In case of non-payment of any such toll on demand, the officers appointed to collect the same may seize any of the carriages or animals on which it is chargeable, or any part of their burden of sufficient value to defray the toll; and, if any toll remains undischarged for twenty-four hours, with the cost arising from such seizure, the case shall be brought before the officer appointed to superintend the collection of the said toll, who may sell the property seized for discharge of the toll, and all expenses occasioned by such non-payment, seizure and sale, and cause any balance that may remain to be returned, on demand, to the owner of the property; and the said officer, on receipt of the property, shall forthwith issue a notice that, at noon of the next day, exclusive of Sunday, or any closed holiday, he will sell the property by auction.

Section 3 (Release of Seized Property): If, at any time before the sale has actually begun, the person whose property, has been seized shall tender the amount of all the expenses incurred, and of double the toll payable by him, the said officer shall forthwith release the property seized.

Section 4 (Exemptions from Toll): No tolls shall be paid for the passage of Police-officers on duty, or of any person or property in their custody, but no other exemption from payment of the toll levied under this Act shall be allowed.

Section 6 (Penalties for Unlawful Toll Collection): Every person, other than the persons appointed to collect the tolls under this Act, who shall levy or demand any toll on any public road or bridge, or for passing through any bazar situated thereon, and also every person who shall unlawfully and extortionately demand, or take any other or higher toll than the lawful toll, or under colour of this Act seize or sell any property knowing such seizure or sale to be to lawful, or in any manner unlawfully extort money or any valuable thing from any person under colour of this Act, shall be liable on conviction before a Magistrate to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six calendar months, or to fine not exceeding two hundred rupees.

Section 7 (Exhibition of Toll Table and Penalties): A table of the tolls authorized to be taken at any toll-gate or station shall be put up in a conspicuous place near such gate or station legibly written or printed in English words and figures, and also in those of the vernacular language of the district, to which shall be annexed, written or printed in like manner, a statement of the penalties for refusing to pay the tolls and for taking any lawful toll.
administration: The State Government may cause tolls to be levied and may place the collection of such tolls under the management of such persons as may appear to it proper; all persons employed in the management and collection of such tolls shall be liable to the same responsibilities as would belong to them if employed in the collection of the land revenue.

title: THE BANKERS ’ BOOK S EVIDENCE ACT, 1891
purpose: An Act to amend the Law of Evidence with respect to Bankers ’ Books.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It has been extended in its application to the whole of the Union territory of Lakshadweep (with effect from 1-10-1967) and to the Union territory of Pondicherry. This Act shall also apply in relation to the Development Banks as if they were a bank as defined in section 2 of this Act.
key_provisions: Section 2A: A printout of entry or a copy of printout referred to in sub-section (8) of section 2 shall be accompanied by a certificate from the principal accountant or branch manager, and a certificate from the person in-charge of the computer system detailing safeguards, data transfer, verification, storage, custody, tampering prevention, and confirming proper system operation and data representation.

Section 4: Subject to the provisions of this Act, a certified copy of any entry in a banker’s book shall in all legal proceedings be received as prima facie evidence of the existence of such entry, and shall be admitted as evidence of the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded in every case where, and to the same extent as, the original entry itself is now by law admissible.

Section 5: No officer of a bank shall in any legal proceeding to which the bank is not a party be compellable to produce any banker’s book the contents of which can be proved under this Act, or to appear as a witness to prove the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded, unless by order of the Court or a Judge made for special cause.

Section 6: On the application of any party to a legal proceeding, the Court or a Judge may order that such party be at liberty to inspect and take copies of any entries in a banker’s book, or may order the bank to prepare and produce, within a specified time, certified copies of all such entries, accompanied by a further certificate that no other relevant entries are to be found. Such an order shall be served on the bank three clear days (exclusive of bank holidays) before the same is to be obeyed, unless otherwise directed.

Section 3: The State Government may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the provisions of this Act to the books of any partnership or individual carrying on the business of bankers within the territories under its administration, provided they keep a set of not less than three ordinary account-books, namely, a cashbook, a day-book or journal, and a ledger.

Section 7: The costs of any application to the Court or a Judge under or for the purposes of this Act and the costs of anything done or to be done under an order of the Court or a Judge made under or for the purposes of this Act shall be in the discretion of the Court or Judge, who may further order such costs or any part thereof to be paid to any party by the bank if they have been incurred in consequence of any fault or improper delay on the part of the bank.
administration: The State Government may extend the provisions of the Act by notification. The Court or a Judge has discretion over the costs of applications and actions under the Act. For investigations or inquiries under sub-clause (iii) of clause (4) of section 2, an order of a Court or a Judge shall be construed as an order made by an officer of a rank not lower than a Superintendent of Police, as specified by the appropriate Government (the Government by which the police officer or other person conducting the investigation or inquiry is employed).

title: THE EXPLOSIVES ACT, 1884
purpose: To regulate the manufacture, possession, use, sale, transport, import and export of explosives.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India and regulates the manufacture, possession, use, sale, transport, import and export of explosives.
key_provisions: Section 5(1): The Central Government may make rules to regulate or prohibit, except under and in accordance with the conditions of a licence granted as provided by those rules, the manufacture, possession, use, sale, transport, import and export of explosives, or any specified class of explosives.

Section 6(1)(a): The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prohibit, either absolutely or subject to conditions, the manufacture, possession or importation of any explosive which is of so dangerous a character that, in the opinion of the Central Government, it is expedient for the public safety to issue the notification.

Section 6A: Prohibits persons who have not completed the age of eighteen years, those sentenced for certain offenses, those ordered to execute a bond for peace or good behaviour, or those whose licence has been cancelled, from manufacturing, selling, transporting, importing, exporting, or possessing specified explosives. It also prohibits selling, delivering, or despatching any explosive to a person known or believed to be prohibited or of unsound mind.

Section 8(1) & 9(1): Requires the occupier of a place, master of an aircraft or vessel, or person in charge of a carriage to give notice of any accident by explosion or fire involving explosives, attended with loss of human life or serious injury, to the Chief Controller of Explosives and the officer in charge of the nearest police-station, within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed by rule. An inquiry into such accidents shall be held by the concerned naval, military, or air force authority, or by the District Magistrate or a subordinate Magistrate.

Section 6F(1) & (4): Any person aggrieved by an order of the licensing authority refusing to grant a licence, varying the conditions of a licence, or suspending or revoking a licence may prefer an appeal to such authority (the appellate authority) and within such period as may be prescribed. Every appeal shall be made by a petition in writing and accompanied by a brief statement of reasons for the order (if furnished) and a prescribed fee.

Section 9B(1): Prescribes punishment for contraventions of rules made under section 5 or of the conditions of a licence granted thereunder: for manufacturing, importing, or exporting any explosive, imprisonment up to three years or fine up to five thousand rupees, or both; for possessing, using, selling, or transporting any explosive, imprisonment up to two years or fine up to three thousand rupees, or both; and in any other case, fine up to one thousand rupees.
administration: The Central Government is responsible for making rules, prohibiting dangerous explosives, and may delegate powers. The Chief Controller of Explosives receives notices of accidents and may be appointed to hold inquiries. Licensing authorities (as prescribed by rules under Section 5) are responsible for granting, refusing, varying, suspending, and revoking licences. District Magistrates hold or direct inquiries into accidents. An appellate authority (as prescribed by rules under Section 5(2)(ee)) hears appeals against licensing decisions. Police officers have the power to arrest without warrant for dangerous offences. Courts are responsible for convicting offenders, imposing punishments, and ordering the forfeiture of explosives.

title: THE RENT RECOVERY ACT, 1853
purpose: To avoid doubts regarding the exercise of jurisdiction transferred by Regulation VIII. 1831, Regulation VII. 1832, and Act VIII. 1835 concerning summary suits for arrears of rent and sales of tenures/lands; to define the proper officers to exercise such jurisdictions, especially where lands are in a district assigned to an independent Deputy Collector or in multiple Collectorates; and to prevent any decision or sale already made from being held invalid on the ground of having been made by an officer of a wrong district.
scope: This Act relates to summary suits for arrears of rent, sales of Putnee Talooks and other saleable tenures, and sales of land in satisfaction of Summary Decrees for rent. It applies to cases where lands are situate in one or more Collectorates, or in districts assigned to independent Deputy Collectors, and extends certain prior Acts and Regulations to sales under Act VIII. 1835.
key_provisions: Section I: If lands subject to sale or rent suit are in one Collectorate, the Collector of that Collectorate conducts the sale or hears the suit. If a Talook or tenure comprises lands in two or more Collectorates, or lands in two or more Collectorates are held under one lease/rent, the Collector in whose Collectorate the greater part of such lands is situate conducts the sale and hears the summary suit.

Section II: If a Collector doubts whether lands or the greater part are within his Collectorate, he shall report the case for the order of his subordinate Board. An order from such Board to proceed shall be conclusive on the question of his jurisdiction.

Section IV: An independent Deputy Collector may, within his Deputy Collectorate, exercise all entrusted powers and jurisdictions of a Collector, and his Deputy Collectorate shall be deemed a Collectorate for this Act's purposes.
Section VI: In cases of sales by an independent Deputy Collector, any notice required to be stuck up at the Cutcherry of the Collector may be stuck up at the Cutcherry of the Deputy Collector.

Section IX: No order, decision, or sale made before this Act's passing, under the aforesaid Regulations or Act, shall be disputed or deemed invalid on the ground of an improper Collector/Officer or Cutcherry, unless proceedings to dispute validity on such ground were commenced prior to this Act's passing.

Section X: Act XXV. 1850, and Section IX. Regulation VIII, 1819 of the Bengal Code, as modified by Clause I, Section XVI. Regulation VII. 1832, and as altered by Act XXV. 1850, are extended to all sales under Act VIII. 1835.
administration: The Act clarifies the roles and jurisdictions of Collectors of Land Revenue, Deputy Collectors, independent Deputy Collectors, and the Board of Revenue in conducting sales and hearing summary suits for arrears of rent. The Board of Revenue decides jurisdictional doubts reported by Collectors.

title: THE RELIGIOUS SOCIETIES ACT, 1880
purpose: To simplify the manner in which certain bodies of persons associated for the purpose of maintaining religious worship may hold property acquired for such purpose, and to provide for the dissolution of such bodies and the adjustment of their affairs and for the decision of certain questions relating to such bodies.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India except "the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States". It does not apply to any Hindus, Muhammadans or Buddhists, or to any persons whom the State Government may from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, exclude from its operation.
