key_provisions: Section 2: Appointment of new trustee in cases not otherwise provided for, by agreement of the body or by a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present at the meeting.

Section 3: Every appointment of new trustees under section 2 shall be recorded in a memorandum under the hand of the chairman of the meeting, in the form set forth in the Schedule, executed and attested by two or more credible witnesses, and requiring registration under the Indian Registration Act, 1877 (3 of 1877), section 17.

Section 4: Property subject to the trust shall forthwith vest in new trustees and old continuing trustees jointly, or wholly in new trustees if no old continuing trustees, without any conveyance or other assurance, upon the same trusts, powers, and provisions.

Section 6: Any number not less than three-fifths of the members may determine to dissolve the body at a convened meeting. In the event of any dispute arising among members, the adjustment of affairs shall be referred to the principal Court of original civil jurisdiction of the district where the chief building is situate, and the Court shall make such order as it deems fit.

Section 7: Upon dissolution, any remaining property after satisfying debts and liabilities shall not be distributed among members, but shall be given to another body for religious worship or other religious/charitable purpose, determined by votes of not less than three-fifths of members present at a meeting, or by the Court in default.

Section 9: Any person interested in a question regarding membership or validity of an appointment under this Act may apply by petition to the High Court for its opinion, which shall be deemed to have the force of a declaratory decree.
administration: The Act is administered by the High Court for opinions on questions (Section 9) and by the principal Court of original civil jurisdiction for disputes arising during the dissolution of societies (Section 6). The State Government has the power to exclude certain persons from the Act's operation by notification in the Official Gazette (Section 1). Appointments of new trustees are recorded by a memorandum under the hand of the chairman of the meeting (Section 3), which requires registration under the Indian Registration Act, 1877 (Section 3).

title: THE EPIDEMIC DISEASES ACT, 1897
purpose: To provide for the better prevention of the spread of Dangerous Epidemic Diseases.
scope: It extends to the whole of India.
key_provisions: Section 2(1): The State Government, when satisfied that the State or any part thereof is visited by, or threatened with, an outbreak of any dangerous epidemic disease, may take measures and prescribe temporary regulations to prevent the outbreak or spread thereof, and determine how expenses (including compensation) shall be defrayed.

Section 2A: The Central Government, when satisfied that India or any part thereof is visited by, or threatened with, an outbreak of any dangerous epidemic disease, may take measures and prescribe regulations for the inspection of any bus, train, goods vehicle, ship, vessel, or aircraft leaving or arriving at any land port or aerodrome, and for their detention or the detention of persons travelling therein.
Section 2B: No person shall indulge in any act of violence against a healthcare service personnel or cause any damage or loss to any property during an epidemic.

Section 3(2): Whoever commits or abets an act of violence against a healthcare service personnel, or abets or causes damage or loss to any property, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term of not less than three months but which may extend to five years, and with a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees.

Section 3A: Offences punishable under sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) of section 3 shall be cognizable and non-bailable. Investigation of such cases shall be conducted by a police officer not below the rank of Inspector and completed within thirty days from the date of FIR registration. Inquiry or trial shall be held as expeditiously as possible, aiming for conclusion within one year.

Section 3E(1) & (2): In addition to punishment, a convicted person shall pay compensation, as determined by the Court, for causing hurt or grievous hurt to any healthcare service personnel. In case of damage to property or loss caused, the compensation payable shall be twice the fair market value of the damaged property or loss, as determined by the Court.
administration: The Act is administered by the State Government (Section 2) and the Central Government (Section 2A) for taking special measures and prescribing regulations. Offences are investigated by police officers not below the rank of Inspector and tried by the Courts (Section 3A), which also determine penalties and compensation (Sections 3, 3E).

title: The Oudh Taluqdárs' Relief Act, 1870
purpose: To relieve from incumbrances the estates of Taluqdárs in Oudh, as many are in debt and their immoveable property is subject to mortgages, charges, and liens.
scope: Applies to taluqdárs in Oudh, defined as persons whose names are entered in the first of the lists mentioned in the Oudh Estates’ Act, 1869, section eight, concerning their immoveable property subject to debts or liabilities (other than those due to Government).
key_provisions: Section 3: The Chief Commissioner may, upon a written application made within twelve months after the passing of this Act by a taluqdár (or their guardian/heir), appoint an officer (Manager) and vest in him the management of the taluqdár's immoveable property.

Section 4: Upon publication of the vesting order, all pending proceedings in Civil Courts regarding the taluqdár's debts/liabilities (excluding Government debts) are barred, processes/executions/attachments become null and void, and the taluqdár/heir are freed from arrest and their moveable/immoveable property from attachment for such prior debts.

Section 6: The Manager shall publish a notice in English and Urdú in the local official Gazette, calling upon all persons having claims against the taluqdár or his immoveable property to notify the same in writing to the Manager within three months from the date of publication.

Section 8: Any debt or liability (other than to Government) not duly notified to the Manager within the specified time shall be barred; however, the Manager may admit such claim within a further period of nine months from the expiration of the initial three months if proof of inability to comply is made.

Section 11: When the total amount of debts and liabilities is finally determined, the Manager shall prepare and submit to the Chief Commissioner a schedule and a scheme for settlement thereof, which, when approved by the Chief Commissioner, shall be carried into effect.

Section 19: The Manager, with the previous assent of the Chief Commissioner, has the power to raise money for debt settlement by demising property by way of mortgage for a term not exceeding twenty years, or by selling a portion of the property by public auction or private contract, with the previous consent of the taluqdár and his heir (if of full age).
administration: The Chief Commissioner of Oudh is responsible for appointing and overseeing the Manager, approving schemes for debt settlement, and making rules (which require approval by the Governor General of India in Council). The Manager, appointed by the Chief Commissioner, is responsible for managing the taluqdár's property, receiving rents, publishing notices to claimants, determining debts, preparing settlement schemes, and raising funds. Appeals against the Manager's decisions under sections seven, eight, or nine lie with the Commissioner of Division within six weeks. The Manager may apply to the Court of the Deputy Commissioner to remove a mortgagee in possession.

title: The City of Bombay Municipal (Supplementary) Act, 1888
purpose: To supplement certain provisions of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, and of the Calcutta Municipal Consolidation Act, 1889, by legislation in the Council of the Governor General for making Laws and Regulations.
scope: This Act supplements the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, and the Calcutta Municipal Consolidation Act, 1889, specifically regarding the jurisdiction conferred upon Appellate Benches of Municipal Authorities, Presidency and other Magistrates, and Courts of Small Causes, and their decisions, orders, and other proceedings. It also establishes procedures for references and appeals to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay concerning these Acts.
key_provisions: Section 1: Confirms the validity of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, and the Calcutta Municipal Consolidation Act, 1889, so far as regards the jurisdiction conferred upon Appellate Benches of Municipal Authorities, Presidency and other Magistrates, and Courts of Small Causes, and their decisions, orders, and other proceedings.

Section 2: Allows the Chief Judge of the Court of Small Causes of Bombay to refer questions of law or usage having the force of law, or the construction of a document, arising from an appeal under section 217 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay for decision. The provisions of sections 618 to 621 of the Code of Civil Procedure (XIV of 1882) apply to such references.

Section 3: Establishes an appeal to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay from a decision passed by the Chief Judge of the Court of Small Causes of Bombay under section 503 or section 504 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, when the amount of the claim exceeds two thousand rupees. The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (XIV of 1882) with respect to appeals from original decrees apply to these appeals.

Section 4: Provides for an appeal to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay from an order passed by a Presidency Magistrate under section 515 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888. The High Court may make rules for regulating the admission and adjudication of such appeals, and the Municipal Commissioner for the City of Bombay must defer action on the Magistrate's order until the appeal is disposed of.

Section 5: Specifies that an appeal to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay under sections 3 or 4 shall, for the purposes of No. 156 of the second schedule to the Indian Limitation Act, 1877 (XV of 1877), be deemed to be an appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure (XIV of 1882) in a case not provided for by No. 151 and No. 153 of that schedule.
administration: information not publicly available

title: THE BENGAL LAND HOLDER’ ATTENDANCE ACT, 1848
purpose: To grant Collectors summary power to impose and levy daily fines on proprietors or farmers of land who omit or refuse to attend or furnish required accounts/documents when summoned, without showing sufficient cause, thereby reducing delays associated with prior confirmation processes by the Government.
scope: Applies to proprietors or farmers of land subject to sundry Regulations of the Bengal Code. This Act does not extend to the North West Provinces of the Presidency of Bengal.
key_provisions: Section I: Collectors may impose a daily fine, not exceeding fifty Rupees, on proprietors or farmers of land who fail to attend or furnish required documents when duly summoned and do not show sufficient cause. This fine is payable daily until compliance and may be levied without further confirmation by the same process as prescribed for the recovery of arrears of revenue.

Section II: The Collector shall forthwith report the imposition and amount of every such fine, and also from time to time the amount levied, to the Commissioner of Revenue, who shall report the same for the information of the local Government.

Section III: Every order passed by a Collector under this Act shall be appealable in the usual manner to the Commissioner of Revenue and other superior authority, but no such appeal shall prevent the levy of any fine so imposed pending the appeal.

Section IV: Whenever the amount levied for any default by authority of a Collector under this Act exceeds five hundred Rupees, the Collector shall report the case specially to the Commissioner of Revenue, and no further levy for such default shall be made otherwise than by authority of the Commissioner of Revenue.
Section V: Nothing in this Act contained shall be deemed to repeal the power of imposing daily fines and of levying the fines so imposed in the manner prescribed by the said several Regulations.
Section VI: The word “Collector” used in this Act shall be taken to mean any person lawfully exercising the powers of a Collector.
administration: The Collector is empowered to impose and levy daily fines. The Collector must forthwith report the imposition and amount of fines, and amounts levied, to the Commissioner of Revenue, who then reports to the local Government. Orders passed by a Collector are appealable to the Commissioner of Revenue and other superior authority. If the amount levied exceeds five hundred Rupees, the Collector must specially report to the Commissioner of Revenue, and further levy requires the Commissioner of Revenue's authority.

title: THE AGRICULTURISTS' LOANS ACT, 1884
purpose: To amend the Northern India Takkavi Act, 1879 (10 of 1879), and provide for its extension to certain other areas.
scope: Section 2(1) extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. The rest of the Act extends in the first instance only to Uttar Pradesh, the Central Provinces, Assam and Delhi and the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in the States of Bombay, Punjab and Ajmer. Any State Government may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the rest of this Act to the whole or any part of the territories to which this Act extends under its administration. The Act came into force on the first day of August, 1884.
key_provisions: Section 4(1): The State Government (or a Board of Revenue or Financial Commissioner, subject to State Government control) may make rules for loans to owners and occupiers of arable land for relief of distress, purchase of seed or cattle, or other agricultural purposes not specified in the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883.
Section 4(2): All rules made under this Act shall be published in the Official Gazette.
Section 4(3): Every rule made by the State Government or a Board of Revenue or a Financial Commissioner under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before the State Legislature.

Section 5: Every loan made in accordance with such rules, all interest (if any) chargeable thereon, and costs (if any) incurred in making or recovering the same, shall be recoverable from the borrower or surety as if they were arrears of land-revenue or costs incurred in recovering the same.

Section 6: When a loan is made to joint-borrowers (e.g., members of a village community) who are jointly and severally bound, a statement on the loan order showing each person's contribution, signed/marked/sealed by them or their agent and the officer, shall be conclusive evidence of their respective contributions.
administration: The State Government or, in a State for which there is a Board of Revenue of Financial Commissioner, such Board or Financial Commissioner, subject to the control of the State Government, is empowered to make rules and administer the Act.

title: THE SHORE NUISANCES (BOMBAY AND KOTABA) ACT, 1853
purpose: to facilitate the removal of nuisances, obstructions and enroachments below high -water mark in the Harbour of Bombay, or upon or about the shores of the Islands of Bombay and Colaba, with a view to the safe Navigation of the Harbour of Bombay, and to the public interests generally.
scope: The Act applies to nuisances, obstructions, and encroachments below high-water mark in the Harbour of Bombay, or upon or about the shores of the Islands of Bombay and Colaba. 'High-water mark' means the ordinary line of high-water at monsoon tides (Section VIII).
key_provisions: Section I empowers the Collector of Land Revenue at Bombay to give notice requiring the removal of any nuisance, obstruction, or encroachment below high-water mark. Such notice must be affixed conspicuously, published in the Bombay Government Gazette, and state that unless removed within one month, the Collector will abate it. The notice may be in Form No. 1 of the Schedule.

Section II allows any person denying the Collector's right to apply by petition to the Supreme Court of Judicature at Bombay within one month after notice, setting forth grounds and praying for restraint. The Court may fix a hearing, require sufficient security for costs, and make orders, including restraining extension or abatement until adjudication.
Section III states that upon the hearing of every such petition, the onus of proving the alleged right shall be on the petitioner.

Section V authorizes the Collector to cause abatement or removal by warrant (Form No. 2 in the Schedule) if no petition is presented within one month, or if it is determined against the petitioner, or dismissed for want of prosecution. The Collector and persons acting under warrant are not answerable for any damage unavoidably occasioned.

Section VI permits the Collector to sell the materials of any removed encroachment or obstruction, applying the proceeds towards payment of removal expenses. Any remaining surplus is forfeited and applied as directed by the Governor of Bombay in Council.

Section VII clarifies that the Act does not prejudice or affect the rights of the East India Company as trustees for the Crown in any part of the Harbour or sea-shore, nor does it preclude or interfere with other civil or criminal proceedings for abating such nuisances and encroachments.
administration: The Collector of Land Revenue at Bombay is empowered to give notice, cause abatement or removal, and sell materials. The Supreme Court of Judicature at Bombay hears petitions challenging the Collector's actions. The Governor of Bombay in Council directs the application of surplus funds from sales.

title: THE DIVORCE ACT, 1869
purpose: To amend the law relating to Divorce and Matrimonial Causes, specifically for persons professing the Christian religion, and to confer upon certain Courts jurisdiction in matters matrimonial.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India except the state of Jammu and Kashmir. (Vide Notification No. S.O. 3912 (E), dated 30th October, 2019, this Act is made applicable to the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and the Union territory of Ladakh.) Relief under this Act is authorized only where the petitioner or respondent professes the Christian religion. Decrees of dissolution of marriage are made only where parties are domiciled in India at the time of petition. Decrees of nullity of marriage are made only where the marriage was solemnized in India and the petitioner is resident in India at the time of petition. Other relief is granted only where the petitioner resides in India at the time of petition.
key_provisions: Section 10. Grounds for dissolution of marriage: A marriage may be dissolved on a petition presented to the District Court by either husband or wife on grounds including adultery, conversion to another religion (ceasing to be Christian), incurable unsound mind for a continuous period of not less than two years, venereal disease in a communicable form for not less than two years, not heard of as alive for seven years or more, willful refusal to consummate marriage, failure to comply with a decree for restitution of conjugal rights for two years or upwards, desertion for at least two years, or cruelty. A wife may also petition if the husband has been guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality.

Section 10A. Dissolution of marriage by mutual consent: A petition for dissolution of marriage may be presented to the District Court by both parties together if they have been living separately for two years or more, have not been able to live together, and mutually agree to dissolve the marriage. A motion by both parties, made not earlier than six months and not later than eighteen months after the petition, can lead to a decree of dissolution if the court is satisfied after inquiry.

Section 19. Grounds of decree (Nullity of Marriage): A decree of nullity may be made on grounds that the respondent was impotent at the time of marriage and institution of suit; parties are within prohibited degrees of consanguinity or affinity; either party was lunatic or idiot at the time of marriage; or a former husband or wife of either party was living and the marriage was in force. The District Court also has jurisdiction to make decrees of nullity of marriage on the ground that the consent of either party was obtained by force or fraud.

Section 22. Judicial separation obtainable by husband or wife: A husband or wife may obtain a decree of judicial separation, on the ground of adultery, or cruelty, or desertion for two years or upwards, by petition to the District Court (Section 23).

Section 27. Deserted wife may apply to court for protection: Any wife deserted by her husband may present a petition to the District Court for an order to protect any property which she may have acquired or may acquire, and any property of which she may have become possessed or may become possessed after such desertion, against her husband or his creditors. The Court may grant a protection order if satisfied of the fact of such desertion, that it was without reasonable excuse, and that the wife is maintaining herself by her own industry or property (Section 28).

Section 36. Alimony pendente lite: In any suit under this Act, the wife may present a petition for expenses of the proceedings and alimony pending the suit. Such petition shall be served on the husband; and the Court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements therein contained, may make such order on the husband for payment to the wife of the expenses of the proceedings and alimony pending the suit as it may deem just. The petition for the expenses of the proceedings and alimony pending the suit, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days of service of such petition on the husband.
administration: The matrimonial jurisdiction is exercised by High Courts and District Courts. High Courts may remove and try suits from District Courts or transfer them to other District Judges. District Courts may refer questions of law to the High Court. All proceedings are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The High Court is empowered to make, alter, and add to rules under this Act, provided they are consistent with the Act and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and are published in the Official Gazette.

title: The Broach and Kaira Incumbered Estates Act, 1877 (Act No. XIV of 1877)
purpose: To relieve from Incumbrances the estates of Thakurs in Broach and Kaira, who are in debt and whose immoveable property is subject to mortgages, charges and liens, by providing for their relief in the manner appearing in the Act.
scope: This Act applies to Thakurs (including taluqdar, Jagirdar, kasbati, and other classes of estate holders as declared by the Local Government) in the districts of Broach and Kaira. It extends to all immoveable property of or to which the debtor is possessed or entitled, or which he is entitled to redeem or acquire, and to all debts and liabilities to which he is subject or which are charged on his immoveable property.
key_provisions: Application for benefit of Act (Section 4): Any Thakur, or any person who would be sole heir or one of the heirs to such Thakur if he then died intestate, may apply, in writing, to the Commissioner within twelve months after the passing of this Act, stating that such Thakur is subject to debts or liabilities and requesting the provisions of this Act be applied to his case.

Effect of order of management (Section 9): On the publication of the order of management, all proceedings then pending in any Civil Court in British India in respect to the debts and liabilities shall be stayed, and the debtor becomes incompetent to contract debts, mortgage, charge, lease or alienate the property under management, or grant valid receipts for the rents and profits.

Notice to claimants and claim submission (Section 12 & 13): The manager shall publish a notice in the Bombay Government Gazette in English and Gujarathi, calling upon all persons with claims against the debtor or property to notify them in writing to the manager within six months. Claimants must present full particulars and deliver all supporting documents, or produce books with entries and copies thereof.

Scheme for liquidation (Section 17): When the total amount of the debts and liabilities has been finally determined, the manager shall prepare and submit to the Commissioner a schedule of such debts and liabilities and a 'liquidation scheme' showing the mode of payment and discharge, which must also provide for payments to be made by the manager under section 11 and may include property improvement.

Power to raise money by mortgage or sale (Section 24): At any time after the liquidation-scheme has been sanctioned, the manager, with the Commissioner's previous assent, shall have power to raise any money required for carrying out such scheme by mortgaging or charging the whole or any part of the property under management for a term not exceeding twenty years, or by selling a portion of the property by public auction or private contract.

Appeal and Revision (Section 29 & 30): An appeal against any decision or order under sections 14, 15, 16, and 22, or imposing a fine or imprisonment under section 35, shall lie to the Commissioner if preferred within six weeks from the date of such decision or order. The Commissioner may also, of his own motion or on application, call for proceedings in any case and pass orders consistent with the Act.
administration: The Act is administered by a 'Commissioner', defined as the Revenue Commissioner of the Northern Division of the Presidency of Bombay. A 'manager', who is typically the Taluqdari Settlement-officer unless otherwise directed by the Local Government, is appointed to manage the property and liquidate debts. The Local Government has powers to make rules, suspend or remove managers, and appoint new ones.

title: THE BOMBAY CIVIL COURTS ’ ACT, 1869
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to the District and other subordinate Civil Courts in the Presidency of Bombay.
scope: This Act extends only to the territories (other than Sind) under the Government of the Governor of Bombay in Council in which the Code of Civil Procedure is now in force. The Governor of Bombay in Council may, by notification in the Government Gazette, extend this Act to any other of the territories under such Government in which the said Code is not in force, or to Sind.
key_provisions: Section 5: There shall be in each District a District Court presided over by a Judge to be called the District Judge, appointed by the Governor of Bombay in Council, and serving as the principal Court of original civil jurisdiction and the Court of Appeal from subordinate courts.

Section 12: The Governor of Bombay in Council may, with the previous sanction of the Governor General of India in Council, appoint a Joint Judge in any District, invested with co-extensive powers and concurrent jurisdiction with the District Judge, except that he shall not keep a file of civil suits and shall transact civil business received from the District Judge or referred by the High Court.

Section 16: The District Judge may refer to any Assistant Judge original suits where the subject-matter does not amount to ten thousand rupees in amount or value, and miscellaneous applications not being appeals. Appeals from Assistant Judge's decrees and orders lie to the District Judge or High Court based on the subject-matter's value (not exceeding or exceeding five thousand rupees, respectively).

Section 24: Subordinate Judges are of two classes: first class with jurisdiction extending to all original suits and proceedings of a civil nature, and second class with jurisdiction extending to all original suits and proceedings of a civil nature wherein the subject-matter does not exceed five thousand rupees in amount or value.

Section 33: The High Court may appoint a Commissioner or Commissioners for a formal and public enquiry into alleged misconduct by any Subordinate Judge, applying the provisions of Act No. XXXVII of 1850, and may order removal, suspension, or reduction in class based on the report.

Section 38: All ministerial officers of the Civil Courts in each District shall be appointed, and may be fined, suspended or dismissed by the District Judge, subject to such rules as the High Court may from time to time prescribe.
administration: The Governor of Bombay in Council is responsible for appointing Judges, altering district limits, and extending the Act. The High Court exercises general control over Civil Courts, prescribes rules for proceedings, fees, and ministerial officers' duties, and conducts inquiries into judicial misconduct. District Judges oversee Civil Courts within their districts, inspect subordinate courts, and manage ministerial staff.

title: THE PUBLIC GAMBLING ACT, 1867
purpose: To provide for the punishment of public gambling and the keeping of common gaming-houses.
scope: Sections 13 and 17 extend to the whole of the United Provinces, East Punjab, Delhi, and the Central Provinces. The State Government may extend all or any of the remaining sections to any city, town, suburb, railway-station, house, and place within three miles of such station-house within the States by notification in the Official Gazette.
key_provisions: Section 1: Defines a “Common gaming-house” as any house, walled enclosure, room or place where instruments of gaming are kept or used for the profit or gain of the person owning, occupying, using or keeping it.
Section 3: Imposes a penalty for owning, keeping, or having charge of a gaming-house, with a fine not exceeding two hundred rupees or imprisonment not exceeding three months.

Section 5: Authorizes a Magistrate of a district, other officer with full magisterial powers, or District Superintendent of Police, upon credible information, to enter and search suspected common gaming-houses, take persons into custody, and seize instruments of gaming, moneys, and articles of value.

Section 8: On conviction for keeping a gaming-house, the convicting Magistrate may order all instruments of gaming found therein to be destroyed, and may order securities for money and other seized articles (not instruments of gaming) to be sold and converted into money, with proceeds and moneys seized to be forfeited or returned at discretion.

Section 11: Grants indemnity to witnesses concerned in gaming who, when examined before a Magistrate on trial for a breach of the Act, make a true and faithful discovery, receiving a certificate and being freed from prosecution under the Act for prior gaming activities.

Section 13: Allows a police-officer to apprehend without warrant any person found playing for money or other valuable thing with instruments of gaming (not games of mere skill) in a public street, place, or thoroughfare, or setting birds/animals to fight, or aiding such fighting. Apprehended persons are brought before a Magistrate and liable to a fine not exceeding fifty rupees or imprisonment not exceeding one calendar month.
administration: The State Government is competent to extend the Act by notification. Magistrates of a district, other officers with full magisterial powers, or District Superintendents of Police are authorized to enter and search suspected gaming-houses. Offences are triable by any Magistrate having jurisdiction. Magistrates can order the destruction of gaming instruments, forfeiture of moneys/articles, and direct portions of fines to informers. Police officers can apprehend individuals without warrant for public gambling offenses. An officer specially empowered by the State Government may compound offenses (Uttar Pradesh Amendment).

title: THE GUARDIANS AND WARDS ACT, 1890
purpose: to consolidate and amend the law relating to Guardian and Ward.
scope: It extends to the whole of India, provided that nothing contained in this Act shall apply to the Renoncants of the Union territory of Pondicherry.
key_provisions: Section 7: Power of the Court to make order as to guardianship. The Court may make an order appointing a guardian of a minor's person or property, or both, or declaring a person to be such a guardian, if satisfied it is for the minor's welfare.

Section 10: Form of application. An application for guardianship, if not made by the Collector, must be by petition signed and verified in manner prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure (14 of 1882), stating particulars such as the minor's name, sex, religion, date of birth, residence, property details, and qualifications of the proposed guardian.

Section 29: Limitation of powers of guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court. A guardian of a ward's property, other than a Collector or testamentary guardian, shall not, without the previous permission of the Court, mortgage, charge, or transfer any immovable property, or lease it for a term exceeding five years or extending more than one year beyond the date on which the ward will cease to be a minor.

Section 34: Obligations on guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court. Such a guardian shall, if required by the Court, give a bond in the prescribed form, deliver a statement of property within six months (or as directed), exhibit accounts, pay balances due, and apply income/property for the ward's maintenance, education, and advancement as directed by the Court.

Section 39: Removal of guardian. The Court may remove a guardian appointed or declared by the Court, or a testamentary guardian, on application or its own motion, for causes including abuse of trust, failure to perform duties, incapacity, ill-treatment, contumacious disregard of the Act or Court order, conviction of an unfitting offence, adverse interest, ceasing to reside within jurisdiction, bankruptcy (for property guardians), or cessation of guardianship under applicable law.

Sections 44 & 45: Penalties for non-compliance. A guardian removing a ward from jurisdiction in contravention of Section 26 is liable to a fine not exceeding one thousand rupees or imprisonment up to six months (Section 44). Failure to produce a minor, deliver statements, exhibit accounts, pay balances, or deliver property/accounts as required by the Court incurs a fine not exceeding one hundred rupees, with further daily fines for recusancy, and detention in civil jail until compliance (Section 45).
administration: The Act is administered by District Courts, which have jurisdiction to appoint or declare guardians, and by subordinate judicial officers empowered by the High Court (Section 4A). The High Court has powers to confer jurisdiction, hear appeals (Section 47), and make rules for the Act's implementation, including procedures for applications, allowances, security, accounts, and investment of ward's money (Section 50). Collectors may be appointed as guardians and are subject to the control of the State Government or an appointed authority (Section 23). The State Government also approves certain rules made by the High Court (Section 50(2)).

title: THE NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT, 1881
purpose: To define and amend the law relating to promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques.
scope: Extends to the whole of India, but nothing contained therein affects the Indian Paper Currency Act, 1871 (3 of 1871), section 21, or affects any local usage relating to any instrument in an oriental language.
key_provisions: Section 13: A “negotiable instrument” means a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer.

Section 64: Promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques must be presented for payment to the maker, acceptor or drawee thereof respectively, by or on behalf of the holder. In default of such presentment, the other parties thereto are not liable thereon to such holder. Presentment through the post office by means of a registered letter is sufficient where authorized by agreement or usage.

Section 117: The compensation payable in case of dishonour of a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque, by any party liable to the holder or any indorsee, shall be determined by rules including the holder being entitled to the amount due upon the instrument together with the expenses properly incurred in presenting, noting and protesting it, and an indorser being entitled to the amount paid with interest at eighteen per centum per annum from the date of payment until tender or realization thereof, together with all expenses caused by the dishonour and payment.

Section 138: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds is an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both, provided the cheque was presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; the payee or holder in due course makes a demand for payment by written notice to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information of unpaid cheque; and the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the notice.

Section 142: No court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint, in writing, made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque, within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises. No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try any offence punishable under section 138.

Section 143A: The Court trying an offence under section 138 may order the drawer of the cheque to pay interim compensation to the complainant, not exceeding twenty per cent. of the amount of the cheque. This compensation shall be paid within sixty days from the date of the order, or within such further period not exceeding thirty days as may be directed by the Court.
administration: Offences under Chapter XVII (dishonour of certain cheques for insufficiency of funds) are tried by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate, and appeals are handled by an Appellate Court. The Act defines the legal framework for negotiable instruments, with enforcement of its provisions generally falling under the purview of the judicial system.

title: THE CALCUTTA LAND – REVENUE ACT, 1856
purpose: To administer the Public Revenues in the Town of Calcutta, specifically by placing the collection of Stamp Duty in charge of the Collector of Calcutta and empowering him to employ Deputy Collectors.
scope: The Town of Calcutta and, for the force of Deputy Collector rules, other parts of the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.
key_provisions: Section I: Regulations modified: Parts of Section VI, Regulation XII, 1826 of the Bengal Code, and Section VI of a Rule Ordinance and Regulation for the Town of Calcutta (June 14, 1827), which prescribe a special appointment by the Governor General in Council for stamp duty collection, are declared subject to modification.

Section II: The collection of the Stamp Duty within the Town of Calcutta shall ordinarily, and unless the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal shall otherwise direct, be in the charge of the Collector of Calcutta.

Section III: It shall be lawful for the Collector of Calcutta to employ any Deputy Collector subordinate to him, in the performance of any part of the duties of his office under the said Regulation, or under Act XI of 1849, or Act XXIII of 1850.

Section III: All Rules, Regulations, and Acts relating to the office of Deputy Collector, shall be of the same force within the Town of Calcutta as in other parts of the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.
administration: The Collector of Calcutta is ordinarily in charge of the collection of Stamp Duty and may employ any Deputy Collector subordinate to him. The Lieutenant Governor of Bengal may direct otherwise regarding the charge of stamp duty collection.

title: THE LAND IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT, 1883
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to loans of money by the Government for agricultural improvements.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. It comes into force in any part of these territories on such date as the State Government may appoint by notification in the Official Gazette.
key_provisions: Section 4: Loans may be granted for making any improvement, which includes the construction of wells, tanks, and other works for water storage/supply/distribution for agriculture, preparation of land for irrigation, drainage, reclamation, protection from floods/erosion, clearance, enclosure, or permanent improvement of land for agricultural purposes, and renewal/reconstruction of such works, or other works declared by the State Government.

Section 5: When an application for a loan is made, the officer receiving it may publish a public notice for objections. The officer must consider all objections and issue a written order. If an objection requires a Civil Court decision, proceedings are postponed until that decision is made.

Section 6: Every loan shall be repayable by instalments (annuity or otherwise) within a period fixed by rules, from the date of actual advance or the last instalment. This period shall not ordinarily exceed thirty-five years, with consideration given to the durability of the work and the expediency of cost payment by the benefiting generation.

Section 7: All loans, interest, and costs, when due, are recoverable by the Collector as if they were arrears of land-revenue from the borrower, from their surety, out of the land for which the loan was granted, or out of collateral security according to the procedure for realization of land-revenue by sale of immovable property. The Collector has discretion in determining the order of recovery modes.

Section 10: The State Government may make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to provide for matters such as the manner of making applications for loans, the officers empowered to grant loans, procedures for inquiries, nature of security, interest rates, conditions for granting loans, inspection of works, payment instalments, and auditing of accounts.

Section 11: When land is improved with a loan under this Act, the increase in value from the improvement shall not be taken into account when revising the assessment of land-revenue on that land. An exception applies to reclamation of wasteland or irrigation of unirrigated land, where the increase may be considered after a period fixed by State Government rules.
administration: The Act is administered by the State Government, which empowers officers (such as the Collector of land-revenue of a district, Deputy Commissioner, or other designated officers) to grant loans, deal with applications, and recover loans. In States with a Board of Revenue or a Financial Commissioner, these bodies may exercise powers conferred on the State Government by sections 4(1), 5(1), and 10, provided that rules made by them are subject to the control of the State Government.

title: THE CENTRAL PROVINCES LAND -REVENUE ACT, 1881
purpose: to consolidate and amend the law relating to Land -revenue and the powers of Revenue -officers in the Central Provinces
scope: all the territories for the time being under the administration of the Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces, except those specified in Part VI of the first schedule of the Scheduled Districts Act 1874
key_provisions: Appeals against decisions or orders under this Act shall lie: (a) from a Revenue-officer subordinate to the Deputy Commissioner (except an Assistant Commissioner exercising Deputy Commissioner powers) to the Deputy Commissioner; (b) from a Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant Commissioner exercising Deputy Commissioner powers to the Commissioner of the division; (c) from the Commissioner of a division to the Chief Commissioner. No third appeal is allowed. Appeals must be filed within 30 days (Deputy Commissioner/Assistant Commissioner), 60 days (Commissioner), or 90 days (Chief Commissioner) from the date of the decision or order (Sections 22, 23).

The assessment of land-revenue on every mahal shall be a definite and separate sum, which may be reduced for up to ten years. The assessment is offered to the entire proprietary body, or to superior or inferior proprietors as determined by the Settlement-officer. Acceptance must be in writing, in a form prescribed by the Chief Commissioner, and delivered to the Settlement-officer. Failure to accept or refuse within a reasonable period may be deemed acceptance by order of the Settlement-officer (Sections 46, 49, 54, 55).

Arrears of revenue payable directly to Government may be recovered by processes including: (a) arrest and imprisonment (not against females, minors, lunatics, or idiots); (b) attachment and sale of moveable property; (c) attachment and direct management of the mahal, share, or land; (d) transfer of the share or land to another malguzar or person with a mortgage/charge (requires Chief Commissioner sanction); (e) annulment of settlement and direct management or farming of the mahal (requires Chief Commissioner sanction); (f) sale of the mahal, share, or land (requires Chief Commissioner sanction); (g) sale of other immoveable property of the defaulter (requires Chief Commissioner sanction) (Section 94).

Any entry in the record-of-rights, after being made over to the Deputy Commissioner, may be corrected by the Deputy Commissioner on application or own motion, only if: (a) all interested persons wish for correction; (b) a suit under section 83 declared it erroneous; (c) it is not in accordance with a Civil Court decree or Revenue/Settlement-officer order; or (d) the founding decree/order was modified on appeal/review or revised by the Chief Commissioner. The Deputy Commissioner may also revise the record-of-rights if provided for therein, exercising powers of the Chief Settlement-officer (Sections 120, 121, 122).

When a local area is under settlement, the Settlement-officer shall list lands appearing to have no lawful owner, issue a notification of intent to demarcate them as Government property, and invite claims within three months. This notification is an advertisement under Act No. XXIII of 1863. The Settlement-officer acts as the Collector under that Act, and claims are dealt with accordingly. If a limited right is established, the Settlement-officer may assign a definite portion of land or, with Chief Commissioner's sanction, compensate the claimant (Sections 40, 41, 42).
administration: The Chief Commissioner, subject to the control of the Governor General in Council, is the Chief Controlling Revenue-authority. Other classes of Revenue-officers include Commissioners, Deputy Commissioners, Assistant Commissioners, Tahsildars, and Naib Tahsildars. The Chief Commissioner appoints, suspends, and removes Commissioners, Deputy Commissioners, Assistant Commissioners, and Tahsildars, and makes rules for Naib Tahsildars (Sections 5, 6, 7, 8).

title: THE INDIAN TRAMWAYS ACT, 1886
purpose: To facilitate the construction and to regulate the working of tramways.
scope: The Act extends in the first instance to "the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States and the territories which were on the 12th March, 1886, respectively, administered by the Governor of Fort Saint George in Council, the Governor of Bombay in Council and the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal." It may be extended to the whole or any part of the said territories by the State Government concerned by notification in the Official Gazette.
key_provisions: Orders Authorizing Construction (Sections 4 & 6): The Government may make an order authorizing tramway construction upon application by a local authority (with road-authority consent) or any person (with local and road-authority consent). The procedure involves the Government publishing a draft order in the Official Gazette, inviting objections/suggestions within a specified date, considering them, and then publishing the final order in the Official Gazette in English and other prescribed languages, which serves as conclusive proof of its making.

Inspection of Tramway Before Opening (Section 12): A tramway, or any portion, extension, or addition thereof, shall not be opened for public traffic until it has been inspected and certified to be fit for such traffic by an engineer appointed by Government.

Grant of Licenses to Third Parties (Section 17): If, after three years of public traffic, a local authority represents to the Government that the public is deprived of the full benefit of a tramway, the Government may, after inquiry, grant a license to any person to use the tramway. Licenses are for a period of 1 to 3 years (renewable), specify the part of the tramway to be used, the number/mode/times of carriages, and the tolls payable to the promoter/lessee and leviable by the licensee.

Cessation of Powers on Discontinuance (Sections 19 & 20): If the working of a tramway or part thereof has been practically discontinued for three months without sufficient reason, the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare the promoter's and lessee's powers to be at an end. Subsequently, the road-authority may, after two months from the notification date, remove the tramway and use materials for road reinstatement, with the promoter liable for removal and reinstatement costs, certified by an officer of the road-authority and countersigned by the District Magistrate.

Future Purchase of Undertaking by Local Authority (Section 22): A local authority, with Government sanction, may require a non-local authority promoter to sell its undertaking within specified times in the order, or within six months after 21 years and every subsequent 7 years, or within two/six months after a discontinuance/insolvency notification (Sections 19 or 21). The sale terms are as specified in the order, or at the then value of the undertaking, excluding profits or compensation for compulsory sale.

Power to Make Rules (Section 24): The Government may make rules for matters including application forms, costs, deposit of money/securities, plans/sections, regulation of motive power, specific matters from Section 7(2), periodical submission of traffic/receipt accounts, accident reporting, and general implementation of the Act. Local authorities and promoters/lessees may also make rules, with Government sanction, for regulating speed, animal power, carriage distances, stopping, lighting, traffic, passenger limits, licensing of staff, and general tramway use.
administration: The Act is administered primarily by the 'Government' (defined in Section 3(16) as either the State Government for tramways wholly within a municipal area or declared not a railway, or the Central Government for other tramways). Local authorities, road-authorities, District Magistrates, and Collectors also have specific powers and functions as defined within the Act.

title: ACT No. XIV OF 1888: An Act to make further provision for the Administration of the Estate of His late Majesty the King of Oudh.
purpose: To make further provision for the administration of the Estate of His late Majesty the King of Oudh, specifically to provide for the mode in which property may be transferred, and suits and other proceedings may be instituted, in the course of the administration of the estate.
scope: The administration of the property left by His late Majesty the King of Oudh, including the settlement and satisfaction of claims against the estate, distribution of remaining property, and the transfer of property and institution of legal proceedings related to the estate.
key_provisions: Section 1(a): The Agent to the Governor General in Council for the Affairs of the late King of Oudh may, in his own name and by his name of office, dispose of any moveable and immoveable property of His late Majesty the King of Oudh in as full and effectual a manner as His Majesty could have disposed of it in his lifetime.
Section 1(b): The Agent may, by his name of office, take a conveyance of any moveable or immoveable property in which His late Majesty had a beneficial interest.

Section 1(c): The Agent may, by his name of office, institute any suit or other proceeding in any Civil, Criminal or Revenue Court in connection with the possession of any moveable or immoveable property belonging to the estate, or the dispossession of any person of such property, or the recovery of rents, debts or other moneys due to the estate, or otherwise in connection with the administration of the estate.

Section 2(a): On the departure from British India, or the death, resignation or removal of an Agent, any moveable or immoveable property vested in him as such Agent shall become vested in his successor in office.

Section 2(b): A suit or other proceeding instituted by an Agent by his name of office may be continued by his successor in office in the same manner as if the departure or the death, resignation or removal had not occurred.
administration: The Governor General in Council has exclusive authority to act in the administration of the property of His late Majesty the King of Oudh. The person holding the office of Agent to the Governor General in Council for the Affairs of the late King of Oudh and for the Purposes of Act XIX of 1887 carries out functions subject to the control of the Governor General in Council.

title: THE BOUNDARY -MARKS, BOMBOMBAY 1846 ACT NO. III OF 1846: An Act for the establishment and maintenance of field boundary marks in the Presidency of Bombay.
purpose: To provide for the establishment and maintenance of permanent marks to distinguish the boundaries of fields, with a view to the better definition and security of landed property, the prevention of encroachments and disputes, and the identification of lands assessed to, or exempted from, the public revenue.
scope: The Act applies within the territories subject to the Presidency of Bombay, specifically concerning the establishment and maintenance of field boundary marks.
key_provisions: Revenue Officers, as entrusted by the Governor in Council, may require Owners or Occupants to erect and maintain field boundary marks of specified materials and number (Section I).

Requisitions for boundary marks shall be served on persons owning or occupying each field according to Form A annexed to this Act, or by posting at the Village Chowree or other conspicuous place if persons are not found (Section II).

In default of Owners or Occupants complying with a requisition, Revenue Officers shall direct the erection and repair of boundary marks, with costs equitably apportioned and charged to the persons with ownership/occupancy rights, or to the village revenues if no such persons are forthcoming (Section III).

Any person convicted of wilfully erasing, removing, or injuring field boundary marks shall be liable to a fine not exceeding Fifty Rupees for each mark, with half awarded to the informer and the other half chargeable with restoration costs (Section V).

Authority for the assessment and realization of sums due under this Act shall be exercised by Revenue Officers in conformity with rules for general Revenue demands, and their proceedings are subject to appeal to subordinate Revenue Authorities (Section VI).

Form A requires the Owner or Occupant of a field to fix or repair boundary marks (e.g., by ridging or raising mounds of earth) within a specified number of days, failing which Government Officers will perform the work and recover costs under Act III of 1846 (FORM A).
administration: The Act is administered by Revenue Officers as entrusted by the Governor in Council, and their proceedings are subject to appeal to the Revenue Authorities to whom they are subordinate.

title: THE BENGAL BONDED WAREHOUSE ASSOCIATION ACT, 1838
purpose: To form a corporate body for the Warehousing of Goods, either in bond or otherwise, by the name of the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association (Section 1).
scope: The Act establishes the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association as a corporate body with powers to sue and be sued, acquire, hold, and transfer property, and manage capital stock and shares. It defines the governance structure, including the election, removal, and authority of Directors, and the conduct of general meetings. The Act also covers financial provisions such as calls for share money, interest on unpaid calls, and the sale of shares for default. Operational aspects include the extension of Act 25 of 1836 to the Association's warehouses, the power to give general security for import/export duties, the fixing of warehousing rates, and the issuance of transferable certificates of deposit. It specifies the liability of proprietors, procedures for increasing capital stock, and the dissolution of the Association. Suits against the Association are to be brought in the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal (Section 29), and Directors must be residents of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal (Section 13).
key_provisions: Section 1: The persons whose names appear in Schedule No. 1 shall, from the 14th day of March, 1838, form a corporate body for the Warehousing of Goods, either in bond or otherwise, by the name of the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association.

Section 6: Any share or shares of the Capital Stock may be transferred by indorsement on the certificate by the proprietor or their attorney, provided the indorsement specifies the transferee's name and is registered in a Register at the Association's office, with a note of registration made on the indorsed certificate by an appointed officer.

Section 10: A rotation among the Directors shall be settled by lot, so that two Directors go out of office on the Monday following the 15th day of May, in every year. On that same Monday, a general meeting of proprietors shall be held to choose two Directors, and no Director going out by such rotation shall be capable of being re-elected until the Monday after the 15th of May in the year next following.

Section 28: As often as any Goods are lodged in any Warehouse of the Association, the Secretary shall deliver a warrant signed by him, in the form set forth in Schedule II, which warrant shall be transferable by indorsement and entitle the holder to receive the specified Goods on the same terms as the original depositor.

Section 31: No Proprietor, his Heirs, Executors, Administrators, Representatives or Assigns, shall be personally liable to any person whatsoever by reason of being a Proprietor; recovery of demands or claims shall only be from and out of the paid up Capital, accumulated Funds, Lands, Messuages, Tenements, Hereditaments and Premises belonging to the Association.

Section 38: The Association may be dissolved by a resolution to that effect of two-thirds in number and value of the proprietors qualified to vote at two successive extraordinary meetings specially called for the purpose, provided not less than three months have elapsed between the first and second meetings.
administration: The business of the Association is managed by six Directors (Section 8), who are elected by a general meeting of proprietors and may be removed by such a meeting (Section 9). Directors serve by rotation, with two going out of office annually on the Monday following May 15th, and successors chosen at a general meeting (Section 10). Directors must be residents within the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal (Section 13). The Directors have authority to expend money for warehouses, make contracts, appoint and remove servants, and generally manage all concerns, subject to Bye-laws (Section 21). They also fix the rates for warehousing goods (Section 27) and can call for share money up to 50% of each share, with further calls requiring a vote of a general meeting (Section 22). The Association's seal must be affixed to any instrument only in the presence and with the consent of three Directors, who must sign it (Section 21). General meetings of proprietors decide elections and questions by a majority of votes, with specific qualifications for voting (Sections 17, 18). The Secretary delivers transferable warrants for lodged goods (Section 28).

title: THE PUNJAB DISTRICT BOARDS ACT, 1883
purpose: To make better provision for local self-government in the Districts of the Panjab, to amend the law for the levy and expenditure of rates on land, and to provide for the constitution of district boards and local boards in those territories, defining and regulating their powers.
scope: The Act extends only to the territories for the time being administered by the Lieutenant-Governor of the Panjab. It comes into force in each district on such date as the Local Government, by notification, directs. Boards established under this Act do not have authority over any portion of a district included in a military cantonment or a municipality. The Local Government may also except any district or part of a district from the operation of all or any provisions of this Act.
key_provisions: Section 5: All land shall be subject to the payment of a local rate, not exceeding one rupee for every rupee of its annual value, with the proportion fixed for each district by the Local Government by notification, or delegated to the district board.
Section 10: The Local Government shall, by notification, establish a district board for each district and may establish local boards within any district, defining their respective authorities.

Section 20(1): District boards are responsible for the control and administration of matters including the management of vested property, construction and maintenance of public roads, establishment and management of public hospitals, dispensaries, sarais and schools, training of teachers, supply and preservation of water, and planting and preservation of trees.

Section 31: A district board may propose the imposition of a tax by resolution, publish a notice defining the tax, consider objections within thirty days, and then submit proposals to the Local Government for sanction. Upon sanction, the board directs the imposition of the tax, fixing a date not less than one month from the meeting date for it to come into force.

Section 39: Every district board shall appoint a finance committee (not less than three members) to submit annual income and expenditure estimates for the next financial year. The board provisionally approves the estimate, which is then sent to the Deputy Commissioner for approval or disapproval. If disapproved, the board may modify it or refer it to the Commissioner, whose decision is final.

Section 51: The Local Government may, by notification stating reasons, declare a district board or local board to be superseded if it is incompetent, persistently defaults in duties, or exceeds/abuses its powers. Upon supersession, all members vacate office, powers and duties are exercised by a person appointed by the Local Government, and property vests in Her Majesty until re-constitution.
administration: The Act is administered by the Local Government, which establishes and oversees district and local boards, fixes rates, sanctions taxes, and makes rules. District boards are responsible for local self-government duties, including managing property, infrastructure, and public institutions, imposing taxes, and managing district funds. Local boards perform duties transferred to them by the Local Government or district boards. Commissioners of divisions and Deputy Commissioners of districts exercise control, supervision, and emergency powers over the boards, including inspecting property, calling for documents, suspending actions, and resolving disputes. The Governor General in Council also has powers to make general rules for taxation and regulate investment powers of district boards.

title: THE MADRAS CITY LAND REVENUE ACT, 1851 (ACT NO. 12 OF 1851)
purpose: To secure the Land Revenue of Madras and ensure that the land revenue accruing due to the East India Company at Madras, within the limits of the Town of Madras, is ascertained and collected in as summary a manner as in other parts of the territories under the Government of the East India Company.
scope: The Act applies to all assessable lands not the property of the East India Company, within the limits of the Town of Madras as defined in Section XII., Regulation II. of 1802, of the Madras Code, concerning land revenue or rent payable to the East India Company.
key_provisions: All assessable lands not the property of the East India Company, within the limits of the Town Madras, of which the rate of assessment is not known or which have not heretofore been assessed, shall be assessed at the rates customarily charged upon lands of a similar description in the neighbourhood (Section I).

Lakiraj tenures of land in Madras, of which uninterrupted possession has been held under alleged grants, exempt or partially exempt from assessment for sixty years, shall be valid; no other lakiraj tenures shall be deemed valid unless held under an unexpired grant from the British Government (Section II).

The Collector of Madras shall determine the rate of assessment, subject to an appeal to the Board of Revenue, to be made within six months from the notification by the Collector of the assessment fixed by him, with the Board's decision being final (Section III).

If any owner of assessed land refuses or neglects to pay upon written demand, the Collector may levy the sum by distress and sale of goods and chattels, wherever found, in the manner appointed for regulating distresses for small rents in Calcutta by Act VII. of 1847, extended to Madras by Section 89, Act IX. of 1850 (Section VII).

Arrears of rent or revenue due to the East India Company are recoverable within six years next after the same are due, or next after an acknowledgment of the same in writing has been given by the person by whom the same is payable, or his Agent, and not afterwards (Section XI).

When a claim to hold land lakiraj, or free of assessment, is set up, the Collector shall inquire into the claim and report to the Board of Revenue. If the Board is satisfied, they make a final order; if not, they direct assessment, leaving the claimant to contest in Civil Courts (Section XII).
administration: The Act is administered by the Collector of Madras, who determines assessment rates, orders land measurements, levies arrears by distress and sale (with powers of a Judge of the Court of Small Causes and authority to appoint bailiffs and appraisers), inquires into claims for rent-free land, and punishes contempts committed in his presence. The Collector acts under the usual control of superior revenue authorities. Appeals against assessment decisions, extra assessments, and contempt orders lie to the Board of Revenue, whose decisions are often final. Claims for rent-free land are reported by the Collector to the Board of Revenue for consideration and final decision.
